title: RULED: routine bead decay is OFF — GC is `bd gc --skip-decay --force`; land the command in .beads/PRIME.md (20 of 39 CLAUDE.md citations already dangle)
description:
RULED 2026-09-09. Routine bead decay is OFF, permanently. The recurring beads-GC command is `bd gc --skip-decay --force`; `--older-than` is never passed again. Full ruling, evidence and both recovery routes are in this bead's notes.

WHY THIS IS NOT JUST A RESTATEMENT. The rule already existed in two memories (`bd-gc-verbs-decay-is-prune-and-restore-does-not-cover-compact`, 2026-09-06; `bd-gc-decay-silently-deletes-closed-beads`, 2026-09-08) and a GC run decayed anyway on 2026-09-08. Memories are not injected into a session. `CLAUDE.md:93` gained a ban clause only on 2026-09-09, buried as a subordinate clause in a bullet about a different trap. `.beads/PRIME.md:64-65` states the hazard but not the command. An operator types a command line; a hazard note does not change what gets typed.

REMAINING WORK ON THIS BEAD — one line, one file. Replace the hazard sentence at `.beads/PRIME.md:64-65` with the literal, copy-pasteable command as the ONLY sanctioned GC invocation:

    bd gc --skip-decay --force      # NEVER pass --older-than; routine decay is OFF (rf2-nj0c)

Keep the existing `bd recall` pointer beneath it. `.beads/PRIME.md` is the right home because it is what `bd prime` serves (a fixed 3,844 bytes, verified), it is read when beads work begins rather than buried in a 77 KB always-loaded file, and it is tracked and allow-listed at the boundary gate. Do NOT add a fourth prose ban to `CLAUDE.md`; do NOT build a wrapper, hook or workflow around `bd gc`.

NOT IN THIS REPO, AND ONLY MIKE CAN DO IT. The authoritative copy of the instruction is Mike's recurring GC prompt. The `14` exists nowhere durable — not in `.beads/config.yaml`, not in `bd config list`, not in any script/hook/workflow, not in Windows Scheduled Tasks, not in Claude settings or jobs. It is typed each run. The PRIME.md edit is a backstop, not a substitute.

THE CLOCK. Today a `--older-than 14` run deletes 0. On/after 2026-09-12 it deletes 48. On/after 2026-09-13 it takes the first surviving `CLAUDE.md` citation (`rf2-9wmqd`). By 2026-09-22 all 18 decay-eligible cited beads are gone. Decay needs a human to type both `--older-than 14` and `--force`, so these are thresholds on the next operator-typed run, not an expiry service.

MEASURED. 20 of the 39 bead ids cited in `CLAUDE.md` no longer resolve — two independent instruments (live `bd show` identity test; export identity set-difference) naming the identical set, with both-direction controls. 14 of the 20 are in Build & Test, 8 of those on lines 140 and 144. All 20 are recoverable in full (114,166 characters).

OUT OF SCOPE: store size and `bd flatten` (ruled under rf2-gwxj); a cited-bead exemption sweep (no `bd pin` command exists at bd 1.2.2); the ~1,006 dangling ids across `spec/` and `docs/`; any CI gate that resolves bead ids. rf2-1r69 is NOT blocked by this decision.

Recovery of the 20 is split out as its own bead and must run only after the prompt change lands.
notes:
--- MAYOR 2026-09-09 AUSEST — THE CORPUS-WIDE NUMBER THE DESCRIPTION DELIBERATELY WITHHELD IS NOW VALIDATED, AND IT IS LARGE ---
The description says the 5798/5275 corpus census was "NOT validated" and that nobody should quote it. I
then validated the part that matters, so the soft number can be replaced by a hard one.

**1018 distinct dangling bead ids are cited in `spec/` or `docs/` prose.** That is the figure to reason
from for the normative tree — not 5275, which spans code comments and generated assets as well.

**THE PATTERN WAS THE THING IN DOUBT, AND IT IS SOUND.** A 20-id random sample of the dangling set was
read back to its citation sites, and every one inspected is a genuine bead reference in human prose:
  * `rf2-006y9b` -> `tools/story/spec/004-Assertions.md:246` and `:267`, inline in normative assertion prose
  * `rf2-00li`   -> two `implementation/adapters/uix/test/**` namespace docstrings, cited as the ruling behind the test
  * `rf2-00zvt`  -> `docs/tools/playground/README.md:1` and `docs/cljs/playground.css:2`, as phase provenance
So the matches are citations, not pattern noise. The ids also LOOK like this tracker's ids across the
sample (`rf2-x76af2.20`, `rf2-2rtt6.12`, `rf2-kufxxe`, `rf2-1xdotm`), including the dotted child form.

**ONE COUNT IN THE DESCRIPTION IS OFF BY ONE THROUGH A KNOWN MECHANISM, AND THE DESCRIPTION'S FIGURE IS
THE RIGHT ONE.** A `git grep -F -f` of the dangling set against `CLAUDE.md` reads **21** where the
description says **20**. `-F -f` matches SUBSTRINGS, so a dangling corpus id that is a prefix of a longer
cited id scores a hit the exact-token method does not. **20 is the sound number** — it comes from
extracting whole `rf2-*` tokens from `CLAUDE.md` and taking a set difference against the tracker, which
cannot be fooled that way. Recorded so the two numbers on this bead are not read as a contradiction, and
as a reminder that `-F -f` is the right instrument for a multi-needle SEARCH (item (e)) but the wrong one
for a COUNT of distinct ids.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE OPTIONS: it prices (c) and (d) upward and leaves (a) and (b) untouched. Restoring
by hand is no longer "roughly 20 identity-selects" if the scope is the normative tree — it is on the order
of a thousand, which is a script rather than an afternoon. **My recommendation is unchanged and is now
better founded: (b), raise retention**, because it is a config change that stops the bleeding immediately
and costs essentially nothing given rf2-gwxj's measured ~55 MB/day accrual against an 8 GB trigger about
two years out. (a) remains the right companion convention going forward whatever is chosen for (b).

--- MAYOR 2026-09-09 AUSEST — CORRECTING MY OWN FIGURE, AND THE NORMATIVE TREE IS THE PLACE THIS ACTUALLY BITES ---
The note above says 1018 dangling ids are cited in `spec/` or `docs/`. **The sound figure is 1012**, and
the method that produced 1018 was the one I had just warned about in that same note.

**WHY 1018 WAS WRONG, WHICH IS THE SAME TRAP TWICE IN ONE SESSION.** I derived it with
`git grep -h -o -F -f <dangling-ids>`, and `-F -f` matches SUBSTRINGS: a dangling id that is a PREFIX of a
longer cited id scores a hit, and with `-o` the printed match is the SHORT id, so it enters the set on the
strength of an appearance it never made. This tracker's dotted child ids make that common — `rf2-kuky.8`
sits inside `rf2-kuky.82`. Re-derived by extracting whole `rf2-*` tokens with a regex and taking a set
difference against the tracker — the same method that gave the sound 20 for `CLAUDE.md` — it is **1012 of
1176 distinct ids cited in `spec/` + `docs/`, i.e. 86% dangling, 164 resolving.** Inflation was only 6, so
nothing in the argument moves; the number is corrected because it is on a bead somebody will quote.

**CONTROLS TAKEN FROM THE DATA IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, not spliced in.** Three RESOLVING ids drawn off the top
of the resolving set were shown at real citation sites — `rf2-1r69` (open) at `spec/005-StateMachines.md:547`,
`rf2-0puue` (closed) and `rf2-22ks` (closed) in `docs/` and `spec/Spec-Schemas.md`. Three DANGLING ids were
shown at real sites AND confirmed absent from the tracker. So the extraction finds live ids where they are,
and the dangling set is dangling.

**THE ONE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT SETTLES WHETHER THIS MATTERS.** `spec/009-Instrumentation.md:2362` — a
NORMATIVE document — defines the two fail-loud arms of `:rf.error/invalid-hiccup-head` and cites beads
inline as the authority for each: "(an XSS-class leak ... per rf2-y1jbaq)", "UNRECOGNISED RESERVED HEAD
(rf2-j81hs)", "Arm (b) is ALSO thrown CLIENT-side by `reagent2.impl.template/parse-tag` (rf2-01zvu)".
`rf2-01zvu` is **absent from the tracker**. So the spec explains an XSS-adjacent guard by pointing at a
record that no longer exists, and a reader asking *why is this arm here, and what may I change about it*
has nowhere to go. **That is the failure mode, stated concretely: not lost clutter, but a normative
sentence whose justification has been collected.**

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE OPTIONS. It does not change my recommendation — **(b) raise retention** — but it
does change who the bead is about. The `CLAUDE.md` half is survivable because that file inlines its
rulings beside the citations. **`spec/` does not consistently do that**: the 009 row above cites three
beads and inlines the reasoning for none of them. So if only one tree is protected, protect `spec/`.

--- MAYOR 2026-09-09 AUSEST — A CONCRETE CASUALTY, FOUND WHILE DOING SOMETHING ELSE, AND IT IS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE ON THIS BEAD ---
The two notes above measure this problem in aggregate. This is one instance, and it is the kind that
makes the aggregate mean something: a ruling was deleted while the thing it protects is still live.

**`rf2-lafmr` IS GONE.** Absent from the tracker and from the current export (control: `rf2-nj0c` reads 1
in the same export). It survived the 2026-08-21 and 2026-09-02 decays — measured `closed|3484` at
`a37a5bf5ac^`, `a37a5bf5ac`, `42ea359b1e^` and `42ea359b1e` — and was deleted by the 2026-09-08 run
(`5e22f68194`). The decay bite is visible in the row counts either side of each: 3781 -> 3163 (the 618 its
commit message names) and 3801 -> 2954.

**WHAT IT CARRIED.** A mayor ruling of 2026-08-21 disposing of two orphan worker branches. Its
`worker/receipts-hic081` arm is **KEEP**, with a stated release condition, because the spike branch is a
LIVE REFERENCE rather than residue — rf2-eoo9 was closed by reading spike commit `fece72f80a` at source
AFTER the spike closed. Its `worker/retire-delete` arm ruled that branch superseded and deletable, and
refuted the filing bead's central claim in the process.

**THE NEAR MISS IS THE POINT.** `worker/receipts-hic081` is still on the remote today. It survived this
tick's hygiene pass **only because `git cherry` reads all-`+` on it and the standing rule is delete-only-
on-`-`** — that is, it was saved by a conservative default, not by anybody being able to read the ruling.
I held it blind this tick and only learned why afterwards, by going and looking. A softer sweep rule, or a
mayor who triaged `+` by subject-matching as the loops doc permits, deletes an artefact whose retention
was deliberately ruled and whose justification had been collected.

**THE RULING IS NOW DURABLE, INDEPENDENTLY OF WHATEVER IS DECIDED HERE.** Recovered verbatim from
checkpoint `42ea359b1e` and stored as the memory **`receipts-hic081-branch-is-deliberately-retained`**,
carrying the keep, the reason, the release condition, and the sibling arm. **Memories are NOT decayed** —
every GC commit message in the log says "memories untouched" — so that copy outlives the next sweep.

WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE OPTIONS ABOVE: it is evidence for **(c)**, exempting cited beads, more than for the
others, because no citation census would have caught this one — the reference that mattered was in a
MEMORY and in the hygiene loop's own procedure, not in tracked prose. But it also shows the cheap
mitigation that needs no ruling at all and that I have just used: **when a ruling protects a live
artefact, put it in a memory, not only in a close reason.** That is worth adopting whatever is decided
about retention.
--- WORKER rulings-a 2026-09-09 AUSEST — THE RULING-FREE HALF IS DONE: 11 OF THE 18 DECAY-ELIGIBLE CITED BEADS ARE NOW PRESERVED IN MEMORIES. THE POLICY QUESTION IS UNTOUCHED AND STILL MIKE'S. ---

This note records insurance, not a decision. Nothing here pre-empts the retention ruling: no policy was
proposed, no `bd gc` wrapper written, no gate added, no automation of any kind, and `CLAUDE.md` was not
edited (the 20 already-dangling citations remain out of scope per the dispatching brief). The work is
correct under every option (a)-(d) above, because **memories are not decayed** — every GC commit message
in the log says so, and the corpus went 990 -> 999 across this session with 0 removals.

## WHAT WAS DONE

All 18 close reasons were read from the FIELD (`bd show <id> --json`), never the rendering. Each was
judged on whether it carries a RULING or a durable measured finding. **11 beads preserved across 8 NEW
memories and 2 UPDATES to existing ones; 7 judged not worth a memory, with reasons below.** Every memory
was verified by effect after writing: read back from `bd memories --json` and compared byte-for-byte
against its source, all 10 identical, 294 backticks intact across the set.

**NEW (8):**

  * `bd-prime-is-overridden-by-beads-prime-md` — rf2-ornb. The override, the hand-sync obligation against

  * `remove-worker-worktree-argument-contract-and-late-refusal` — rf2-u62e. The absolute-path contract,

    stdout-canary-blocks mechanism that made a `tail -6` show six CANARY_AFTER lines and no explanation.
  * `spawn-onto-occupied-fixed-actor-id-ruling` — rf2-dokz. The ruling, the four source-cited "why not"

    masked-plant lesson, and rf2-xjee needing a ruling before code moves.

**UPDATED IN PLACE (2), both because the standing memory was thinner or WRONG:**
  * `mid-path-glob-pathspec-returns-a-silent-zero` — rf2-uwvv. **The standing memory was actively

## NOT PRESERVED (7), each with its reason

  * **rf2-i834** (163 chars) — a throwaway probe bead. Fully covered by `reopening-a-bead-erases-its-

  * **rf2-p0b0** (1945) — its entire substance IS the memory `a-name-axis-search-cannot-see-a-derived-

  * **rf2-kdaw** (342) — CLAUDE.md inlines the whole finding, and the load-bearing filename fact

  * **rf2-3r2t** (3157) — covered by TWO existing memories, one of which (`mkdocs-strict-reaches-spec-
    only-via-the-docs-yml-staging-step`) is a deliberately-kept correction that names this bead and
    carries both the hook-stages-on-any-invocation finding and the complementary-gates pairing.
  * **rf2-s4dp** (1966) — a landed bug fix (a no-op `:abort-fn` closure leaving two ghost handles), not
    a ruling. The behaviour is pinned by a test with a red control that names the defect, which is the
    right home for it.
  * **rf2-kuky.8** (1526) — the decision (`rf/sensitive?` ships as `boolean`, never `true?`, so a
    producer stamping a string/keyword/1 cannot be treated as not-sensitive) is carried in the SHIPPED

## THREE FINDINGS THE DISPATCHING BRIEF ASKED FOR

**(1) NO CLOSE REASON READ 0 CHARACTERS.** All 18 carry text, 163 to 5891. In particular `rf2-dokz`
(5856) and `rf2-z5lv` (5891) — which CLAUDE.md records as having been erased by an audit reopening on
2026-09-08 — have been re-closed with full reasons, so nothing extra is unrecoverable on that account.

**(2) A CLOSE REASON CAN BE STALE ABOUT ITS OWN BEAD, AND ONE OF THESE IS.** `rf2-dokz`'s close reason
ends "A `spec/005` SENTENCE IS STILL OWED". It is not: a LATER note on the same bead records that PR
#9517 carried it in, verified on trunk at `spec/005:3022`. Preserving the close reason alone would have
minted a false obligation, so the memory records the paragraph as LANDED. This is the preamble's rule
about reading by mutation time rather than by position, met in the wild — and it is a reason not to
mechanise any future rescue of close reasons: the notes can overtake them.

**(3) THE CLOCK IS CLOSER THAN "14 DAYS" SUGGESTS, BECAUSE THE CADENCE HAS COLLAPSED.** GC run dates:
2026-08-21, 2026-09-02, 2026-09-05, 2026-09-08 — intervals of 12, 3 and 3 days. Measured on the export
at `5e22f68194^`, that last run deleted only the 5 rows closed 2026-08-22/23, so the tracker's floor is
now **2026-08-29, eleven days old**, sitting hard against the retention line with **90 beads in the
2026-08-29/30/31 band** as the next thing to cross it. Of the 18, the nearest is **rf2-9wmqd (closed
2026-08-30T10:22Z), which reaches 14 days on 2026-09-13** — i.e. roughly the run after next at the
current three-day cadence. rf2-y1jkm and rf2-3r2t follow on 2026-09-16. So the margin on this set was
one to two GC runs, not weeks.

## WHAT REMAINS AT RISK

  * **The 7 unpreserved beads' provenance**, deliberately. Each is covered in substance; what decays is
    the pointer, which is exactly the cost option (a) accepts.
  * **The NOTES of every preserved bead.** Only the close reasons were distilled. `rf2-dokz` alone
    carries 43,139 characters of notes containing the full ruling analysis, and `rf2-9wmqd` carries
    50,980. The memories capture the load-bearing conclusions, not the working. Where the reasoning
    itself is load-bearing it was lifted (the four "why not" facts, the position table); the rest goes.
  * **The wider tree, which this pass does not touch at all.** The notes above measure 1012 of 1176
    distinct bead ids cited in `spec/` + `docs/` as already dangling, including the
    `:rf.error/invalid-hiccup-head` row at `spec/009:2362`. Nothing here helps that; only a retention
    decision does.
  * **The `merged-pr-audit-*` writer is still live.** `merged-pr-audit-pr-9532` appeared in the memory
    corpus DURING this session, which independently corroborates rf2-ornb's finding that the generated
    out-of-repo harness is still running. Per that ruling it authorises deleting nothing.

## STILL WHOLLY MIKE'S

The retention question — (a) accept and stop citing bare ids, (b) raise retention, (c) exempt cited
beads, (d) restore the 20 by hand — is **untouched by this pass and is not pre-empted by it**. This
work makes options (a) and (b) cheaper and does not argue for either. The 20 already-deleted beads
remain permanently gone; no memory can bring them back, which is why this half did not wait.

--- MAYOR 2026-09-09 AUSEST — §2 REPRICING: THE CLAIM IS EXACTLY RIGHT, AND THE FRAMING UNDERSTATES IT. THIS IS A LEAK, NOT A BACKLOG. ---
I re-measured this bead's headline before reporting "still held" a fourth time, because a count is the
thing that goes stale first. It has NOT gone stale — and the second measurement, which nobody had
taken, changes what the decision is about.

**THE HEADLINE IS CONFIRMED TO THE DIGIT.** `grep -oE 'rf2-[a-z0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?' CLAUDE.md | sort -u`
reads **39** distinct cited ids; resolving each through `bd show --json` and checking the document is
an ARRAY (not the error-object shape a bad id returns) gives **19 resolve / 20 dangle**. The bead says
"20 of the 39 ... no longer resolve". Correct as written.

**THE MEASUREMENT NOBODY HAD TAKEN — AGE OF THE SURVIVORS. ALL NINETEEN ARE 9 DAYS OLD OR YOUNGER.**

    age 0d : rf2-dokz, rf2-g2br, rf2-i834, rf2-ornb, rf2-z5lv
    age 1d : rf2-2e8f, rf2-mfzw, rf2-uo5f
    age 2d : rf2-kuky.8, rf2-uwvv
    age 3d : rf2-kdaw, rf2-p0b0, rf2-s4dp, rf2-u62e
    age 4d : rf2-dttg
    age 6d : rf2-3r2t
    age 7d : rf2-y1jkm
    age 9d : rf2-9wmqd
    (plus rf2-fmst, which is OPEN and so not subject to decay at all)

**Not one survivor is older than 9 days, and not one casualty is younger than 14.** That is not a
coincidence and it is not a partially-broken corpus that has settled: it is the exact signature of a
14-day decay working perfectly, sampled mid-drain. The 20 already gone are simply the ones that aged
past the line.

**WHAT THAT MEANS FOR THE DECISION, and it is the whole point of this note.** The dangling count is
not a static 20 to be cleaned up once. **On present behaviour every one of the 19 survivors dangles
within 14 days** — the first (`rf2-9wmqd`) in **5 days**, then `rf2-y1jkm` in 7, `rf2-3r2t` in 8 —
and CLAUDE.md ends up citing **39 dead ids out of 39**. Any option that repairs the existing 20
without changing what happens at day 14 buys roughly a fortnight and then the file is worse than it
is now, because the repaired citations will have been re-broken by the same mechanism.

**SO THE OPTIONS ARE NOT EQUALLY PRICED, and I am NOT ruling — this is yours.** What the measurement
says is that a repair-only option is a treadmill: the citations decay as fast as they can be fixed.
An option that changes the decay behaviour (or that stops CLAUDE.md depending on bead ids resolving)
is the only one whose cost does not recur every fortnight. I have deliberately not re-argued your
options (a)-(d) here — just priced the clock they all sit on.

**NOTHING IS RED AND NOTHING IS BLOCKED.** No gate resolves bead ids, so this costs nothing today; the
cost is that CLAUDE.md's own worked examples stop being checkable, and that is what erodes. Two beads
([[rf2-gwxj]] and [[rf2-1r69]]) are recorded as staying open until this is ruled.

**INSTRUMENT NOTE.** Resolve each id by asking `bd show <id> --json` and testing `type == "array"`.
A CR-suffixed id — which is what `jq -r` hands a `while read` loop on this box — returns an ERROR
OBJECT on stdout with exit 1, and `.[0]` then dies with "Cannot index object with number", which a
`2>/dev/null` turns into a uniform false answer for every id. Strip the CR and check the shape.

## RULED 2026-09-09 — routine bead decay is OFF, permanently. The GC command is `bd gc --skip-decay --force`.

**THE DECISION.** The recurring beads-GC instruction becomes `bd gc --skip-decay --force`, and `--older-than` is never passed again. Routine decay is off permanently. NOT lengthened to bd's 90-day default: that deletes nothing for ~79 days and then does precisely what 14 days did, against a corpus by then far larger, converting a known 20-bead loss into a future unwatched mass loss. NOT a cited-bead exemption sweep (option c) — deferred, see OUT OF SCOPE. The dossier and the Codex Recommendation independently reached the same policy; where they conflict I have taken the corrections recorded below, all of which are Codex's and all of which narrow the urgency without touching the conclusion.

**THE DEADLINE, numerically.** Today, 2026-09-09, a `--older-than 14` run deletes **0** beads (the tracker floor is 2026-08-29, 11 days back). On/after **2026-09-12** such a run deletes **48**. On/after **2026-09-13** it takes the first surviving `CLAUDE.md` citation, `rf2-9wmqd` (closed 2026-08-30). By **2026-09-22** all 18 decay-eligible cited beads are gone; the 19th survivor, `rf2-fmst`, is OPEN and therefore not decay-eligible at all. So the fuse is **three days** to the first non-zero bite and **four** to the first citation. Decay is not automatic — see the `--force` note under ANALYSIS — so this is a fuse on the next operator-typed run, not a countdown clock.

---

## THE CRUX — WHERE THE INSTRUCTION MUST LIVE

## RECOVERY PROCEDURE FOR THE 20 — two routes, both proven read-only today

**`bd restore` DOES NOT RECOVER A DECAYED BEAD.** It pairs with `bd admin compact` and requires an existing compacted issue row; it is not undelete. The commit message on `d7d7b61dcc` (2026-07-17) — *"decayed 9524 closed beads (restorable via `bd restore`)"* — is **wrong**, and any future reader who trusts it will conclude the data is safe when it is not.

**ROUTE 1 — `bd history`. Preferred: one command, no git, no path mangling.** This is the Codex Recommendation's find and it is correct; the dossier missed it entirely and proposed only Route 2. Verified today on the decayed `rf2-83z0`: `bd --readonly history rf2-83z0 --limit 2 --json` returned **2 snapshots** carrying description **2956** / notes **4040** / close_reason **3317** characters — byte-for-byte the figures the git route yields — despite `bd show` failing on the same id. ```bash

bd --readonly history <id> --limit 5 --json | jq -r '.[] | "\(.Issue.status) desc=\(.Issue.description|length) notes=\((.Issue.notes//"")|length) close=\((.Issue.close_reason//"")|length)"'

title: bug(pair-skill): experiment loop restores the post-dispatch epoch, so compared handlers start from different state
description:
## Scope

Correct the canonical commit-and-compare procedure in `skills/re-frame2-pair/references/recipes.md` so every handler version is exercised from the same retained frame-state. Reconcile the smallest carrier set that teaches or pins this procedure: the recipe, its prompt regression, and any Pair README/meta wording needed to keep one coherent workflow. Preserve the current `restore-epoch!` contract and the preference for `dispatch-dry-run` when no committed comparison is needed.

## Correctness finding

The recipe says the manual experiment holds the starting `app-db` constant, but it captures the epoch produced BY the baseline dispatch and restores that same epoch before running the edited handler. `restore-epoch!` restores a named record's canonical `:frame-state-after`, not its `:frame-state-before`. The restore therefore reinstalls the baseline event's POST-state. The edited handler runs from an already-mutated frame, so the two epochs do not share a starting state and their difference cannot be attributed solely to the code edit.

This is the canonical live-runtime validation workflow, not a wording nicety: following it can compound non-idempotent state, produce a false patch verdict, and then present that verdict as a controlled experiment.

## Evidence

- `skills/re-frame2-pair/references/recipes.md:213` promises “same starting app-db, same event, only the code changes.”
- `recipes.md:217` tells the agent to dispatch first and capture the `:epoch-id` from the resulting record. Lines 219-223 then restore “the captured epoch”; lines 230-231 dispatch the edited handler and compare the two results.
- `spec/Tool-Pair.md:112` specifies that `(rf/restore-epoch! frame-id epoch-id)` restores the named epoch's whole `:frame-state-after`. `spec/API.md:644` repeats the same contract.
- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/tool_pair.cljc:1017-1049` binds `recorded-frame-state` from `(:frame-state-after epoch)` as the only restore source and installs it.
- `implementation/epoch/test/re_frame/epoch_test.clj:2830-2838` explicitly pins that restoring a record restores its `db-after`, not its `db-before`, and says callers must restore an earlier epoch to rewind past a mutation.
- The Pair README already demonstrates the correct concept at `skills/re-frame2-pair/README.md:130-134`: restore `<pre-click-epoch-id>` before retrying.
- Pair-MCP's rollback guidance likewise names the preceding head: `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/test/re_frame2_pair_mcp/dispatch_dry_run_test.cljs:634-650` instructs manual recovery through `:before-epoch-id`.
- Current prompt regression is non-discriminating. `skills/re-frame2-pair/tests/prompts/prompt_regression_test.clj:118-123` merely requires `dispatch-and-collect`, `restore-epoch`, and `reg-event`; lines 618-625 require the dedicated restore-tool spelling but never assert which epoch id it receives. The incorrect procedure is green.
- The same procedure has a nearby capture error: `recipes.md:229` says `handler-meta` should differ from “what you captured at step 1”, but step 1 captures only the result epoch, not handler metadata. Separating the state anchor, result epoch, and handler fingerprint resolves this without expanding scope.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Begin at retained epoch E0 with app-db `{:n 0}`.
2. Register a baseline handler that increments `:n` by 1.
3. Follow recipe step 1. Dispatching records E1 with `:db-before {:n 0}` and `:db-after {:n 1}`; capture E1 as instructed.
4. Follow recipe step 3 and restore E1. The frame is still `{:n 1}`, because E1's `:frame-state-after` is the restore source.
5. Replace the handler with one that adds 2 and dispatch again. The result is `{:n 3}`.
6. Under the promised common starting state E0, the edited handler's result would be `{:n 2}`. The observed 3 includes the baseline run's mutation, so the comparison is confounded.

Append, toggle, consume-once, and other non-idempotent handlers exhibit the same problem, and repeated iterations compound it. The existing warning about HTTP/navigation/storage effects is necessary but orthogonal: this defect is in the supposedly rewindable frame-state itself.

## Required invariant

The baseline handler and every edited handler must receive the same whole pre-dispatch frame-state. The epoch containing a run's result is comparison evidence; it is never the rewind anchor for recreating that run's input.

## Recommended minimal fix

- Before the baseline dispatch, read and capture the operating frame's current retained head as `pre-dispatch-epoch-id`. Separately capture the current handler fingerprint if later reload/re-registration verification will compare it.
- Dispatch the baseline and retain its RESULT epoch for outcome/diff evidence only.
- Before every edited comparison run, call the dedicated `restore-epoch` tool with `pre-dispatch-epoch-id`, verify `:restored? true`, then modify/verify and dispatch. Repeat the same restore before subsequent iterations.
- If the frame has no retained pre-dispatch epoch, or the anchor has aged out of the bounded ring, refuse this commit-and-compare procedure or use `dispatch-dry-run` when one consequence answers the question. Never silently substitute the baseline result epoch.
- Correct the handler verification step to reference the separately captured pre-edit fingerprint rather than claiming step 1 captured it.
- Keep the whole-frame restore warning and the escaped-side-effect warning exactly in force.

Use the smallest existing epoch-read form/tool that exposes the current head; no new public framework or MCP API is required merely to correct this recipe.

## Non-goals

- No change to `restore-epoch!` semantics, epoch storage, or ring retention.
- No new restore-before API, transaction/sandbox abstraction, generalized experiment framework, or compatibility layer.
- No claim that external effects can be undone; HTTP, navigation, storage, timers, and other escaped host work remain explicit caveats.
- No replacement of the manual loop when the programmer genuinely needs two committed epochs; `dispatch-dry-run` remains the preferred simpler path for a one-off consequence.
- No broad rewrite of unrelated Pair recipes or tool surfaces.

## Related / duplicate search

All-status `.beads/issues.jsonl` searches over title, description, and notes covered `experiment loop`, `same starting state`, `same starting app-db`, `pre-dispatch epoch`, `pre-event epoch`, `wrong epoch`, `captured epoch`, `commit-and-compare`, `pre-click-epoch-id`, and restore combined with baseline/result. No bead owns this restore-anchor defect.

- Closed `rf2-1f60u` fixes `tail-build` comparing against a post-edit handler probe; it does not address the pre-event frame-state anchor.
- Closed `rf2-k2qus` is a stale-vocabulary hygiene sweep.
- Closed `rf2-tnmuq` reconciles the `eval-cljs` posture.
- Closed `rf2-p1keh` removes cross-process Story composition.

`git blame` shows the capture-result/restore-result sequence has persisted since commit `344754178f` (2026-06-03), while later changes updated the restore wording around it. `git log -S'Rewind to the captured epoch'` shows no repair. The README's older `pre-click-epoch-id` example is an internal contradiction, not an implementation of the correct procedure in the canonical recipe.

## Uncertainty

The exact lowest-friction existing read used to obtain the current epoch head should be selected while implementing against the current tool catalogue. The correctness invariant is not uncertain. A new frame may have no predecessor and a bounded ring may evict it; those cases require an honest refusal/fallback, not invented rewindability.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The canonical experiment procedure captures a `pre-dispatch-epoch-id` before the baseline dispatch and restores that id before every compared dispatch. The baseline RESULT epoch is named separately and used only as outcome/diff evidence.
2. No current Pair instruction states or implies that restoring the epoch produced by an event recreates that event's starting state.
3. A focused worked regression starts from `{:n 0}` and proves baseline `+1 => 1` and edited `+2 => 2`. Reintroducing the current result-epoch restore produces 3 and makes the control fail.
4. A missing, aged-out, or rejected pre-dispatch anchor fails honestly before the edited live dispatch; the workflow does not substitute another epoch or claim a controlled comparison.
5. The handler fingerprint is captured separately before re-registration/source edit, and the verification step references that actual capture.
6. The existing prompt regression for “Experiment loop” requires pre-event/pre-dispatch anchor semantics and distinguishes the restore anchor from the resulting epoch id, while retaining the dedicated `restore-epoch` tool assertion.
7. README, recipes, and relevant prompt/meta carriers agree on the corrected sequence; existing Pair prompt/runtime gates remain green.
8. The fix adds no framework/MCP API, history mechanism, side-effect rollback, or generalized experiment abstraction.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9225 (branch worker/skpair-a).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA. 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 met as written. AC 3 (the worked

title: Reject remote open-in-editor callers that spoof a loopback Host
description:
## Problem

`re-frame.testbed.open-in-editor-server/local-request?` authenticates a request as local from its `Host` header and optional `Origin`, but never checks the TCP peer exposed by Ring as `:remote-addr`. `Host` is supplied by the client, and a direct HTTP client may legitimately omit `Origin`, so a non-loopback peer can send `POST /__rf-open-in-editor` with `Host: localhost:<port>` and pass the guard.

This is a reachable boundary failure, not a hypothetical proxy configuration. All 14 handler-wired `:dev-http` entries in `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn` omit `:host`. The source inside the pinned `thheller/shadow-cljs` 3.4.10 jar defaults that missing host to `0.0.0.0`, while its Ring adapter places `(str (.getRemoteAddress request))` in `:remote-addr`. Thus the testbeds listen beyond loopback and already provide the transport fact the guard needs.

After the guard, `handle` resolves the caller's `file` and calls `launch!`; absolute paths pass through and any existing path can launch the developer's editor. A reachable network peer can therefore trigger editor/Node processes repeatedly and probe coarse path/launch outcomes. CORS does not protect this route from a direct client.

## Evidence

- `tools/testbed-support/src/re_frame/testbed/open_in_editor_server.clj:399-407`: `local-request?` destructures only `headers`; its docstring claims locality from loopback Host/Origin.
- The same file at `:479-508` calls that check before resolving the requested path and invoking `launch!`; `resolve-file` at `:93-112` explicitly passes absolute paths through.
- `tools/testbed-support/README.md:63-69` documents the endpoint as local-only.
- `tools/testbed-support/test/re_frame/testbed/open_in_editor_server_test.clj:68-77` builds requests without `:remote-addr`; tests around `:130-149` reject non-loopback/missing Host but cannot exercise a remote peer spoofing a loopback Host.
- `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn` contains 14 `:dev-http` entries using this handler and no `:host` setting. The installed, lock-pinned shadow-cljs 3.4.10 source was inspected: `start-build-server` uses `"0.0.0.0"` when host is absent, and the AOT Ring adapter supplies the remote socket address.
- Ring's request-map specification defines `:remote-addr` as the client or last proxy IP: https://github.com/ring-clojure/ring/blob/master/SPEC.md

A minimal failing regression is a request map with `:request-method :post`, a valid existing file, `"host" "localhost:8031"`, no Origin, and a non-loopback `:remote-addr`; current code reaches the launch spy instead of returning 403.

## Recommended shape

Make the endpoint's one central launch guard require a loopback transport peer in addition to the existing Host/Origin checks. Parse the concrete Ring/shadow representations deliberately (including IPv4 and IPv6 loopback), fail closed when the peer is missing or malformed, and do not trust forwarding headers: these shadow dev servers are direct listeners. Keep this narrow; there is no need for tokens, sessions, middleware, or a redesign of the testbed API. Update the request fixture to provide a loopback peer by default and document the transport check alongside the existing local-only contract.

Targeted searches of `.beads/issues.jsonl` and this path's git history found no current owner for remote-peer validation or Host spoofing. Commit `4e6f05d33c` introduced the Host/Origin guard intending to cover public binding/DNS rebinding, but did not inspect `:remote-addr`; this completes that intended boundary rather than duplicating the coordinate, cwd, or tier-classpath work.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A POST from a non-loopback `:remote-addr` returns 403 before path resolution or process launch even when `Host` is loopback and Origin is absent or loopback.
2. Missing and malformed peer addresses fail closed; do not consult `X-Forwarded-For` or similar client-controlled headers.
3. Direct IPv4 and IPv6 loopback peers continue to support the existing cross-port local testbeds, Host validation, and optional loopback-Origin behavior.
4. Focused tests cover the spoofed-Host/non-loopback-peer case and assert the launch spy is untouched, plus accepted IPv4/IPv6 loopback representations actually emitted/allowed by the Ring adapter.
5. The testbed-support README's security contract mentions the peer-address requirement, and `clojure -M:test` from `tools/testbed-support/` plus `npm run test:testbed-support` pass.
close_reason:
Fixed by PR #9198 (https://github.com/day8/re-frame2/pull/9198).

The premise held. `local-request?` destructured only `:headers` and never consulted `:remote-addr`, so a POST from 203.0.113.7 carrying `Host: localhost:8031` with no Origin answered 200 with the launch spy fired against `file=/etc/passwd`. That exact assertion is now the regression test, and it was red before the change (25 assertions red across the new tests, 0 after).

`loopback-peer?` now gates the whole endpoint on Ring's `:remote-addr`, ahead of the method branch and the OPTIONS preflight. The Host/Origin check is retained as non-authoritative defence in depth (it still narrows a loopback peer's browser to same-machine pages and closes DNS rebinding).

Accepted set, each with a reason recorded in the docstring: all of 127.0.0.0/8 (a client may connect to any of it; the kernel never routes it off-box); `::1` AND its expanded spelling `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`; and the IPv4-mapped `::ffff:127.0.0.1`.

CORRECTION to the description's mechanism detail. The pinned adapter is thheller/shadow-undertow, whose `exchange->ring` fills `:remote-addr` from `(.getHostAddress (.getAddress (.getSourceAddress exchange)))` — a BARE numeric literal — not `(str (.getRemoteAddress request))` as the description states (verified in the installed 0.3.1 and 0.3.4 sources; identical in both). That distinction matters: `getHostAddress` emits IPv6 loopback EXPANDED as `0:0:0:0:0:0:0:1`, so a check for the `::1` spelling alone would have refused every genuine IPv6 caller. It also means no port is ever appended, so a `host:port` value is refused.

Missing and malformed values fail closed, and `X-Forwarded-*` is ignored (a `:dev-http` server is a direct listener). Parsing runs only on strings already shaped like numeric literals, because `InetAddress/getByName` resolves `localhost` — measured 3ms — and any attacker-chosen name pointing at 127.0.0.1, to a loopback address; an unguarded parse would have been a second way in.

Workflow note: running a testbed off-box no longer works by pointing a browser at it. The seam documented in the README is an SSH local port-forward (`ssh -L 8031:localhost:8031 <host>`), which presents a genuine loopback peer and needs no configuration; the default was not widened.

Gates: `clojure -M:test` from `tools/testbed-support/` — exit 0, 41 tests / 228 assertions before; exit 0, 47 tests / 295 assertions after. `scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci` exit 0, with a planted broken target confirming it returns exit 1 and names the line. `npm run test:testbed-support` was declined for want of `implementation/node_modules` in the worker worktree — its `:ns-regexp` selects only `.cljs` suites and this diff touches no `.cljs` file (the server namespace is `.clj` and never enters a browser or Node bundle); CI runs it on the PR.

title: surface-review(http): frame-scope managed request cancellation and supersession
description:
## Scope

Correct the frame isolation of implementation/http managed-request lifetime tracking: raw app-authored :request-id supersession, :rf.http/managed-abort, and actor-destroy cancellation. Keep the public :rf.http/managed args map and :rf.http/managed-abort effect shape unchanged.

## Correctness finding

The HTTP registry is process-global but both of its cancellation indexes use frame-local identifiers without the frame: in-flight is request-id -> handle and actor-in-flight is actor-id -> handles. managed-handler correctly captures the issuing frame, yet passes the raw request-id to next-issuance! and supersede!. managed-abort-handler receives frame-ctx but deliberately ignores it and aborts by the raw id. The actor-destroy hook likewise accepts only actor-id. Consequently two isolated frames running the same application code are not isolated at the managed-HTTP lifetime boundary.

A frame B request using the same ordinary stable id as frame A supersedes and suppresses A's live request. A manual abort dispatched in B can abort A even when B owns no request. Generated/fixed actor ids are also frame-local, so destroying an actor in one frame can walk the same actor-id slot containing another frame's handles. This is especially exposed by documented per-request SSR frames, Story/test variants, and side-by-side mounts: reusing code naturally reuses ids such as :articles/load.

## Steps to Reproduce

From implementation/http on current tip, the following read-only registry probe records a frame-A handle, then exercises the same production supersede selector a frame-B managed-handler calls:

  clojure -M -e "(require '[re-frame.http.registry :as r]) (r/clear-all-in-flight!) (let [seen (atom []) _ (r/record-in-flight! :shared nil {:frame :frame/a :abort-fn #(swap! seen conj [:frame/a %])})] (println (pr-str {:before (select-keys (r/lookup-in-flight :shared) [:frame]) :cross-frame-supersede-found? (boolean (r/supersede! :shared)) :aborts @seen :after (r/lookup-in-flight :shared)}))) (r/clear-all-in-flight!)"

Exit 0 output:

  {:before {:frame :frame/a}, :cross-frame-supersede-found? true, :aborts [[:frame/a :request-id-superseded]], :after nil}

A second probe invokes the real abort effect handler with frame B's context over frame A's registered handle:

  clojure -M -e "(require '[re-frame.http.registry :as r] '[re-frame.http.handlers :as h]) (r/clear-all-in-flight!) (let [seen (atom []) _ (r/record-in-flight! :shared nil {:frame :frame/a :abort-fn #(swap! seen conj [:frame/a %])})] (h/managed-abort-handler {:frame :frame/b :event [:cancel]} :shared) (println (pr-str {:caller-frame :frame/b :aborts @seen}))) (r/clear-all-in-flight!)"

Exit 0 output:

  {:caller-frame :frame/b, :aborts [[:frame/a :user]]}

This is not merely a test helper artifact. transport/run-attempt! publishes every live/backoff handle through registry/record-in-flight! using the raw normalized request-id; handlers/managed-handler calls supersede! with that same raw id before each fresh issuance.

## Source evidence

- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/handlers.cljc:207-220 and 253-267 capture :frame in the normalized context, proving frame identity is available.
- handlers.cljc:381-410 nevertheless calls next-issuance! and supersede! with request-id alone.
- handlers.cljc:413-428 names managed-abort-handler's first arg _frame-ctx and calls abort-in-flight! with request-id alone.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/registry.cljc:36-73 defines process-global atoms keyed only by request-id and actor-id.
- registry.cljc:87-179 clears, looks up, and aborts by unqualified request-id; 201-289 keys issuance and supersession the same way.
- registry.cljc:391-428 aborts actor work by actor-id alone, while the hook contract receives no frame.
- implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/transport.cljc:1082 and 1701 are the live/backoff record-in-flight! sites; handles carry :frame, but the lookup key does not.
- spec/014-HTTPRequests.md:790 promises replies remain in their issuing frame; docs/core/frames.md:138-140 defines SSR and repeated mounts as isolated worlds. The lifetime side channel currently breaks that same isolation before reply routing.
- The repository already proved this class for higher-level consumers: commit 450cdd44a1 (rf2-sxyrzk) had resources/mutations synthesize [:rf.req frame-id work-id] because the process-global HTTP registry otherwise cross-cancelled identical frame-local work ids. That workaround does not protect direct :rf.http/managed users, whose ergonomic API accepts ordinary stable ids.

## Recommended bounded repair

Make the issuing frame part of HTTP's internal cancellation identity while preserving the caller's raw :request-id as the public correlation value echoed in replies and traces. Thread frame through request lookup/supersede/manual-abort/issuance and through actor-destroy cancellation (or use an equivalent compound internal key). A programmer should be able to write :request-id :articles/load once in reusable app code; the runtime, which already carries frame identity, should provide isolation automatically.

Keep the existing process-global atoms if compound keys are the smallest repair. Reuse the existing identity-conditional cleanup, retry handoff, finalisation CAS, and frame-destroy sweep. Update Spec 014 and internal comments that currently describe request-id keying as process-global to state the intended same-frame supersession law. Existing resource-generated qualified ids may remain if removing that redundant qualification would broaden the change; compatibility matters less than keeping this repair focused and mechanically safe.

## Posture rationale

This is a correctness and ergonomics repair, not extra machinery. Requiring every direct HTTP caller (and AI-generated app code) to remember to bake a frame id into an otherwise simple stable request id leaks a runtime implementation detail and makes reusable event code unsafe in the exact multi-frame/SSR modes the library advertises. Internal compound identity uses information already present and keeps the public API minimal. Do not add namespaces, registries, lease objects, user-facing tokens, or configuration switches.

## Non-goals

- No new public request-id type, frame argument, cancellation verb, failure kind, or compatibility alias.
- No transport, retry, decode, privacy, reply-envelope, or stale-trace redesign.
- No requirement to move process-global atoms into every frame; correct compound keying is sufficient.
- No attempt to make explicit cross-frame cancellation possible through this local effect. If such orchestration is ever needed, it deserves a separate explicit surface rather than accidental raw-id reach-through.
- No cleanup of the resources workaround unless required to keep its current behavior green.

## Related and duplicate search

Searched all-status beads with bd search/list across titles and descriptions for request-id, managed HTTP, in-flight registry, frame isolation, cross-frame, frame-qualify, frame-scope, supersede, and abort. No current or closed bead owns direct managed-HTTP cross-frame cancellation. The closest current HTTP issues are closed rf2-rsv2n (abort during body preparation), closed rf2-o9e15 (supersede-test flake), and closed rf2-lddbk (successful response metadata); all are distinct.

History search found commit 450cdd44a1 / historical rf2-sxyrzk, which fixed only resources and mutations by pre-qualifying their generated transport ids and explicitly documented the still-process-global HTTP registry. Commit d4f85afcac added frame-destroy aborts but its tests use distinct request ids per frame. The existing spec/conformance/fixtures/http-managed-frame-isolation.edn uses canned replies with no :request-id, so it never enters this registry. The full implementation/http JVM suite is green (506 tests, 3882 assertions, 0 failures/errors), confirming the current suite lacks this adversarial same-id/two-frame case rather than contradicting the reproduction.

## Uncertainties

The minimal internal signature migration needs care because resources calls the late-bound abort-by-id seam with its already-qualified token, and machines currently calls the actor-destroy hook with actor-id alone. The implementer should choose whether those internal hooks gain frame-id or accept a compound selector while leaving app-facing effects unchanged. CLJS is single-threaded but the same key collision exists; JVM/SSR additionally needs existing atomic/identity-conditional cleanup preserved under concurrent frames.
acceptance_criteria:
- A deterministic direct-managed-HTTP test creates two live frames, issues overlapping requests with the same raw :request-id in both, and proves both remain live; neither receives :request-id-superseded merely because the sibling frame reused the id.

- Frame destroy and epoch restore still abort every handle owned by the selected frame, including two sibling frames that reused a request id; retry-backoff handles remain continuously cancellable and clean only their own registry entry.
- App-visible replies/traces continue to echo the caller's original :request-id, not an internal compound key. Existing single-frame request-id, abort, supersede, retry-race, actor-destroy, and resource/mutation qualified-id tests remain green on JVM and CLJS.

- Spec 014 and API/docs describe same-id supersession and managed-abort as frame-scoped, consistent with the isolated-world frame contract, without asking callers to manually qualify ids.

## Verdict (PR #9195)

PREMISE HOLDS, and was reproduced at tip before any edit. Spec 014 was SILENT
on cancellation scope — it said neither "frame-scoped" nor "process-global" —
so this settled the contract and implemented it (outcome 2 of the three the
dispatch named).

### Reproduced at tip (afe446ea71 / 835ea4804f), all four probes exit 0

- `supersede!` driven from frame B resolved and aborted frame A's handle:
  `{:cross-frame-supersede-found? true, :aborts [[:frame/a :request-id-superseded]], :after nil}`
- `managed-abort-handler` with frame B's ctx aborted frame A's handle:
  `{:caller-frame :frame/b, :aborts [[:frame/a :user]]}`
- `abort-on-actor-destroy :actor/x` aborted BOTH frames' handles.
- FOURTH finding the bead did not record: the issuance counter was shared too —
  frame B's FIRST issuance under a shared raw id read **2**, not 1, perturbing
  B's `:work/id` for a supersession that never happened to it.

### Contract settled against 014

Frame-scoping was chosen because process-global contradicts what 014 already
says: §Frame awareness promises multi-frame apps "work without extra
ceremony" (false unless every caller hand-qualifies ids); §Chain order and
frame scope already makes the sibling HTTP surface — the interceptor chain —
per-frame; §Sibling actors are not affected already asserts inter-actor
isolation. Spec 014 gains §Frame scope — a `:request-id` is frame-local, a
§Frame scope note under Abort on actor destroy, §Frame awareness extended from
reply routing to request lifetime, and the snapshot helpers' new arities.

### Fix

The issuing frame is now part of the INTERNAL key (`[frame-id id]`) for both
indexes and the issuance counters, derived from the `:frame` stamp the
transport already puts on every handle. Public `:rf.http/managed` args map and
`:rf.http/managed-abort` effect shape unchanged; the caller's raw
`:request-id` stays the correlation value echoed in replies and traces. No new
namespace, registry, lease object, user-facing token or config switch.

### Acceptance criteria

Met: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and the registry half of 4. Witness is
`implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_frame_scoped_cancellation_test.clj`
(9 deftests, deterministic — latched localhost `HttpServer`, no timing-
sensitive assertion). AC 7's negative control was run: restoring raw global
keying takes the suite to exit 1 / 21 failures / 3 errors with 7 of the 9 new
deftests red; reverted and verified by blob hash.

### Deliberately NOT done — see rf2-wjfm

AC 4's "the actor-destroy hook carries enough frame identity to make this
structural" needs the HOOK'S CALLERS to pass a frame, and both are outside the
dispatched fence: `machines/lifecycle_fx/finalize.cljc`
`abort-actor-in-flight-http!` (its caller in `destroy.cljc` has `frame-id`
bound one line above) and `core/frame.cljc` ~3983's machines-absent fallback.
The registry half IS done — the actor index is keyed `[frame-id actor-id]` and
`abort-on-actor-destroy` has a frame-bearing 2-arity — so the follow-up is one
line per call site. Its `[actor-id]` arity is retained as the documented
ANY-FRAME sweep so no flag day is needed. Filed rf2-wjfm (P2,
discovered-from rf2-o8ek) with both call sites named.

The resources any-frame seam (`:http/abort-in-flight!`) was left unchanged and
is correct as-is: its token is already frame-qualified
(`[:rf.req frame-id work-id]`, Spec 016), so at most one frame can match.

### Gates (captured exits, never read through a filter)

- `implementation/http` `clojure -M:test` BEFORE: exit 0, 506 tests / 3882 assertions
- same AFTER, on the final rebased base: exit 0, 515 tests / 3929 assertions

- `python -m mkdocs build --strict`: exit 0
- `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py`: exit 0, and proven live — a planted broken
  anchor took it to exit 1 naming file, line and the planted anchor.

### Two test seeds needed a frame; neither was a production regression

Both production `record-in-flight!` sites stamp `:frame (:frame ctx)` from a
ctx whose value came through `require-frame-stamp!` (throws on nil), so a real
handle can never lack one. `flows_http_integration_test.clj`'s
`prime-in-flight!` and the `managed_http_counter` example's demo-only seed fx
both built handles by hand without it; the example already BOUND the carried
frame for its deferred dispatch and simply did not put it on the handle.
REOPENED by merged-PR audit of #9195 (2026-09-04). The compound registry keys correctly isolate the main managed-abort/supersede paths, but two cleanup paths still escape that scope:

1. `examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs` was changed to stamp `:frame` on its seeded handle, yet its `:abort-fn` still calls one-arg `(clear-in-flight! request-id)`. #9195 redefined that arity as an ANY-FRAME sweep. With the demo mounted in frames A and B under its stable `:http-counter/long` id, cancelling A invokes A's abort closure and deletes BOTH registry slots; B's fake long request becomes unregistered/unabortable and its UI can remain loading. A deterministic JVM registry probe using that exact closure shape produced `{:aborts [[:frame/a :user]], :a-live? false, :b-live? false}`. The new frame-lifecycle test explicitly notes that one-arg clear would take the sibling slot, but the changed example was not given the same handle-cell/identity-exact cleanup it models.

2. `clear-in-flight!`'s 2-arg nil-handle branch also delegates to the ANY-FRAME sweep. Both live-fetch host paths acknowledge a publication window between `record-in-flight!` and `reset! handle-holder`; on the JVM another thread can fire the just-published abort-fn there. A nil handle from frame A can therefore delete an already-live same-id frame-B slot. The comment that the window "precedes any successor" covers only same-frame succession, not a sibling frame that was already live.

Keep rf2-wjfm as the existing owner of the deliberately deferred actor-hook call sites. On this owner, make every cleanup path that possesses an issuing frame frame-exact, including the demo and nil/publication path, and add same-id/two-frame witnesses for both. Do not broaden the public effect API or remove the resource token's intentional any-frame seam.
REOPENED by merged-PR audit of #9202. The cross-frame cleanup paths are fixed, but the new frame-exact fallback does not close the publication race across the registry TWO indexes. record-in-flight! publishes the stamped handle to in-flight first (registry.cljc:142-143), then actor-in-flight in a separate swap! (144-146). A JVM abort between those swaps invokes the handle while its forward-reference cell is still nil; clear-in-flight-in-frame! removes the request slot and tries to remove the actor slot before that slot exists, then record-in-flight! resumes and publishes the already-aborted handle into actor-in-flight. Deterministic same-thread watch interleaving on current tip printed {:abort-fired? true, :request-slot nil, :actor-slot-count 1}. This is the exact publication window #9202 calls production-reachable from another JVM thread, for actor-originated requests carrying both ids. The result is a ghost actor handle, stale introspection and retained state until later actor/frame teardown. Preserve the frame-scoped and identity-conditional laws, but make publication plus cleanup coherent across both indexes (or make the stamped handle identity available to the abort closure before either publish). Add a controlled midpoint interleaving witness asserting both indexes are empty after the abort; the landed tests call cleanup only after record-in-flight! has finished and therefore cannot see this gap.
## Round 3 verdict (PR #9251) — the #9202 audit finding

PREMISE HOLDS, reproduced at tip (150805f821) before any edit with the
audit's own recorded output, byte for byte:

  {:abort-fired? true, :request-slot nil, :actor-slot-count 1}

Governing note confirmed by probe rather than by reading the title: at the
LAST closed snapshot notes=6241, newest=7667 — 1426 characters written while
closed, so the newest note is the audit and it governs. Control rf2-y1jkm
varied across the same walk (status and notes length both moved).

### Fix

record-in-flight! publishes to in-flight and actor-in-flight in two swap!s
over two atoms. Cleanup cannot close the gap between them — it cannot remove
a slot the future has not written — so PUBLICATION observes it instead,
using the identity law the rest of the registry already runs on: once both
swaps are done, if this handle is no longer the one in-flight holds under its
key, a cleanup or a supersession overtook publication and the handle is
retracted from the actor index by identity. Only a handle carrying BOTH ids
spans two swaps, so only it is reconciled; both the check and the removal
match on identical?, so neither a same-id successor nor a sibling frame can
be touched. remove-from-actor-index! moved above record-in-flight! so the
reconcile can call it. Public API, effect shapes and the echoed raw
:request-id are unchanged; no spec edit warranted (Spec 014 already carries
the frame-scope law from #9195 and says nothing about publication ordering).

After: {:abort-fired? true, :request-slot nil, :actor-slot-count 0}.

### Also measured, and it bounds the severity

The ghost is confined to the ISSUING frame — a sibling live under the same
raw request-id AND actor address kept both slots
({:aborts [[:frame/a :user]], :b-request true, :b-actor-count 1}). #9202's
frame-scoped keys hold; this was an incoherence within one frame.

### Witness

Four deftests appended to
implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_frame_scoped_cancellation_test.clj.
An atom's watches run on the swapping thread BEFORE swap! returns, so a watch
firing the abort the instant the request slot appears interleaves strictly
between the two publications — decided, not raced. The landed tests could not
see this gap because each calls cleanup only after record-in-flight! returns.
Three assert both indexes empty (abort door, supersede door, and with a
sibling frame live); the fourth is the control that an undisturbed
publication is never retracted, which an unconditional reconcile would fail.
Each carries a precondition assertion so a case whose interleaving stopped
happening fails rather than passing vacuously.

Negative control: removing the reconcile and nothing else takes the suite to
captured exit 1 / 3 failures — exactly the three ghost assertions, with the
fourth correctly still green. Byte-copied before, cmp-verified on restore.

### Example checked, NOT changed

examples/core/managed_http_counter/core.cljs is correct at tip: it stamps
:frame and its :abort-fn calls the frame-exact clear-in-flight-in-frame!
(#9202's repair for the previous round). It also seeds with actor-id nil, so
it publishes into ONE index, has no midpoint, and cannot reach this finding.
check-examples-compile.cjs therefore not a gate for this diff.

### Gates (captured exits, re-run on the final rebased base)

- implementation/http clojure -M:test: exit 0, 525 tests / 3969 assertions
- npm run test:cljs: exit 0, 11,220 tests / 56,708 assertions
- npm ci from the lockfile in the worker worktree; node_modules verified
  populated (103) rather than trusting the reported exit

### For a further carrier — the residual is rf2-ni74, NOT this bead

The OTHER door is blind at the same midpoint: abort-on-actor-destroy landing
between the two swaps finds no actor slot and fires nothing, so the handle
survives its actor's destroy. Measured:
{:case :actor-destroy-at-midpoint, :abort-fired? false,
 :request-slot-present? true, :actor-slot-count 1}.
That is a MISSED ABORT, not an incoherent index — a different class from the
ghost closed here, still swept by the later frame-destroy/epoch paths, and
JVM-only. Do NOT 'fix' it by reversing the publication order: that only moves
the blind door onto :rf.http/managed-abort by request-id, the primary
app-facing verb, which currently works in this window. A real fix needs
cross-atom atomicity, which should be weighed against the width of the window
before it is built. Filed rf2-ni74 (P3, discovered-from rf2-o8ek) with the
probe and that reasoning.

rf2-wjfm remains the owner of the deferred actor-hook call sites; untouched.

title: realworld: the Global Feed renders zero articles - silently, while Popular Tags from the same demo backend populate (pilot 1's nominated screen)
description:
FOUND 2026-09-03 ~17:40 AUSEST by the rf2-t4jpz PRE-PILOT rehearsal, running the
OPERATOR half of docs/design/hicasso/product/pilots/workspace.md at pin
6e9bb105fc9b1569d63fdebc212b7787a2a023ba.

SYMPTOM. The RealWorld/Conduit example's Global Feed renders NO ARTICLES. The
page shows the RealWorld empty state, "No articles are here... yet.", and it
never changes. Nothing complains: 0 page errors, 0 console errors of any level
(the only two console messages are React DevTools' banner and shadow-cljs'
"#6 ready!"), 0 failed or 4xx requests, and the stylesheet resolves (52 rules).
#app innerHTML is 2350 characters - the same number the previous operator run
recorded and read as a pass.

WHY IT MATTERS. The feed is pilot 1's FIRST NOMINATED SCREEN. brief-realworld.md
tells the blinded pilot "it works today. Run it before you change anything" and
then asks it to migrate "the feed" to Hicasso. A pilot meeting an empty feed has
no article card to port, no before/after to compare, and a false premise in its
own brief. This is not scaffolding the operator got wrong - it reproduces from a
workspace assembled literally from the manifest, with every step green.

THE POPULAR TAGS SIDEBAR ON THE SAME PAGE RENDERS, and that is the discriminator.
Tags come back through the SAME in-page demo backend and the SAME
:realworld.demo/http-stub override of :rf.http/managed (realworld_http/http.cljs),
and they populate: intro, demo, clojure, re-frame. So the stub is installed, the
managed-HTTP path works, and the demo world has articles in it (the tag list is
derived from the seeded articles' :tagList - demo_backend.cljs line 544-545 -
so a populated sidebar PROVES the seed corpus is present and reachable).
Whatever fails is specific to the article-list read.

MEASURED, four ways, all on one build and one server:
  /                            #app 2350, empty feed, 0 errors
  /realworld                   #app 2350, empty feed, 0 errors
  click "Home" (route-link)    URL unchanged, still empty, 0 errors
  click the "clojure" tag      URL -> /realworld/tag/clojure, heading shows
                               "clojure", STILL "No articles are here... yet."
The tag click is the important row: the route matched WITH its path param (the
heading proves it), so :realworld/home-tag's :on-match [[:home/load]] fired,
and :home/load's own :fx dispatches [:tags/load] and [:articles/load] together
(tags.cljs). Tags updated. Articles did not.

NOT A BASE-PATH ARTEFACT. routing.cljs:254 wires
(routing/with-base-path routing/history-url-strategy "/realworld"), so the app
is served from a sub-path in the repository's own example site. The workspace
serves public/ at the root of :dev-http instead. That mismatch is real and is
filed separately, but it is NOT this: the tag row above is at a URL where the
base path is correct, and the feed is empty there too.

NOT AN ERROR PATH. The view renders the machine's :empty state, not its error
state, so :articles/load-failed did not fire and :articles/error is nil. The
fetch "succeeded" and produced nothing.

THE BEHAVIOURAL BASELINE CANNOT SEE THIS, which is why it has survived. Both
pilot baselines are green at this pin (realworld npm test exit 0, Ran 4 tests
containing 123 assertions, 0 failures). But baseline_test.cljs drives
:articles/load with :fx-overrides {:rf.http/managed :realworld.test/canned-articles}
- CANNED replies, not the demo backend - so it asserts the slice fills from a
reply it supplied itself and never exercises demo_backend/handle at all. Examples
are test-free by policy and no CI lane renders this app, so nothing in the tree
watches this screen.

ROOT CAUSE NOT PINNED. Two candidates were opened and neither closed: the
demo backend's dispatcher matches the article list with
(str/ends-with? path "/articles") after stripping the query (demo_backend.cljs
:438, path-of/query-params at :385ff), and paged reads :limit/:offset back out
of the query string via query-int. Either could be it; so could something above
them in :rf.http/managed. Left for the fix dispatch rather than guessed at here.

REPRODUCE. Assemble pilot 1's workspace per workspace.md steps 1-4 at this pin,
npx shadow-cljs watch app, load http://localhost:8080/ in a browser and read the
Global Feed. Expect the empty state beside a populated Popular Tags sidebar.
