  clojure -M:clein pom       # the same command the preflight runs
  # then read target/classes/META-INF/maven/<group>/<artifact>/pom.xml BY EYE

Three corrections to how the dossier framed it, all Codex, all right:
  - Use an ISOLATED CHECKOUT that preserves the layout, not a scratch copy of one tool
    directory: a lone directory loses ../../VERSION and the git context derived preflights
    read.
  - You cannot rehearse all three against Clojars before the first tool tag -- xray needs
    machines-viz PUBLISHED, story needs xray. Stage each rehearsal behind its prerequisite.
  - Local packaging proves local output; it never proves remote publication.

Where the automation already reads the pom, do not duplicate it by hand: xray
(preflight-xray-package.sh:234), story (preflight-story-package.sh:188), mcp-base and
story-mcp (preflight-tool-package.sh:126, :303) all assert their expected dependency sets.
MACHINES-VIZ HAS RESOLUTION BUT NO GENERATED-POM PREFLIGHT -- which is exactly why the
human read matters most at tag 1, where the automation is thinnest. (The dossier's "only a
human pom read catches this" was overstated for the other four; Codex is right, and it
sharpens rather than defeats the case for reading tag 1.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: implementation/fresco
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: implementation/fresco. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.15 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.15 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.15 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.15) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/fresco. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/fresco. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/fresco to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/fresco; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/fresco plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/fresco that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Test-suite pruning, fifth pass: implementation/schemas
description:
Child of rf2-nvxtm (test-suite pruning, fifth pass). One worktree, one PR.

SURFACE: implementation/schemas. This is the surface of rf2-txsk5.26 (fourth pass). Read rf2-txsk5.26 first: its description, notes and close reason. Together they give the runners and lanes, the count floors, the surface's cautions, the covers it relied on, and what the fourth pass already pruned. rf2-txsk5.26 gives the exact files in scope, or names the third-pass bead (rf2-n6gq4.26) that does. Confirm the scope and the runners yourself at tip in step 1, and report the delta.

<DIR> in the prompt below means this surface.

REPO MECHANICS: read rf2-nvxtm's description. Its count-floor, CLJS-lane, test-name, cross-surface-cover, hot-zone, plant and one-PR rules apply in full, and they win over anything in the prompt that seems to conflict.

== THE PROMPT (verbatim from Mike's local prompt file, which is not checked in; also in rf2-nvxtm's description)

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/schemas. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/schemas. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/schemas to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/schemas; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/schemas plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/schemas that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside migration codemods (from-re-frame-v1 and reagent-to-fresco) that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: Live default frame: an ambiguous route is silently dropped from route matching; make it loud
description:
Follow-up to rf2-bmrh9 (PR #11235), blocked on it. Under the ruling, a frame made without `:images` resolves the registration store live, and an id registered from more than one namespace raises `:rf.error/ambiguous-registration` WHERE IT IS USED, loudly, while every other id keeps working. rf2-bmrh9's worker reported two places where the shipped behaviour falls short of that. Re-derive both at tip after rf2-bmrh9 merges.

1. SILENT: enumerations leave ambiguous ids out, so a route table built on one of these frames silently lacks the ambiguous route, and a URL that should match it falls through without any error. Make it loud: either keep the route in the table and raise `:rf.error/ambiguous-registration` when it matches, or emit the always-on record when the table is built. Pick the smaller change and say why.
2. INCONSISTENT: a dispatched event or `:fx` with an ambiguous id is reported on the always-on axis and skipped, which is how an unknown id behaves. But an ambiguous subscription, cofx or interceptor THROWS, where an unknown sub emits a record. Inside a render, that is the difference between an error record and a crashed view. Where the unknown-id path for that kind exists, route the ambiguous case through the same path, so the programmer sees one behaviour per kind. Where a kind has no such path, keep the throw and say so. rf2-bmrh9 could not do this because implementation/core/src/re_frame/subs.cljc was fenced off; it is free now. rf2-9q37u also edits subs.cljc (one `:recovery` value), so sequence the two or cluster them.

Recorded and NOT to be done here: a framework standard registered AFTER an application registration of the same id wins silently, because the `reg-*` refusal cannot fire in that order. Framework standards load first in practice, so under the stance this stays a known edge.

Gates: failing-first tests through the public `rf/make-frame` (red before, green after), the core and routing JVM lanes, and `npm run test:cljs` under a granted build lane if a `:cljs` branch changes.

Routing it through the unknown-id record path would be consistency polish, which the stance says not to litigate. Item 1 STANDS, because it is a silent failure: an ambiguous route dropped from route matching raises nothing, which the ruling exists to prevent. WORKER RESULT (2026-10-15 10:22:26 AUSEST), PR #11242 (draft until gates were in, then marked ready), branch worker/routing-ambiguous from origin/main f58f426632.

CAUSE, measured at base: a frame made without :images enumerates only the ids it can run, so its route table (built from rf.registrar/registrations :route) lacked a route id registered from two namespaces. With /page registered from two namespaces and a catch-all /* present, [:rf.route/handle-url-change "/page"] landed on the catch-all with no error, and match-url inside the frame returned nil.

FIX, raise-at-match. A new internal rf.registrar/ambiguous-registrations kind returns, under a bound live view, the {id {ns descriptor}} of the ids the enumeration leaves out because they are ambiguous, and {} otherwise. route-table keeps every registration of such an id as a pair marked ::ambiguous (built per call, uncached). When a marked pair is the winning match, match-url calls rf.registrar/lookup, which throws the canonical :rf.error/ambiguous-registration. match-url-fail-closed still fails it closed to :rf.route/not-found (:reason :match-error), and first reports it through emit-error-both! against the navigation event in flight, with :failing-id = the route id, the same shape as the fx ambiguity record. redact-declared-url now matches quietly, so egress projection does not report again. With that planted back, one navigation produced 1142 records instead of 1.

WHY NOT EMIT AT TABLE BUILD: on a live-store frame the table is rebuilt on every match-url call, including egress re-matches, so emitting there fires on unrelated navigations, several times each. It also leaves a lower-ranked route silently serving the URL.

EVIDENCE: new implementation/routing/test/re_frame/routing_ambiguous_route_test.clj, 2 tests / 10 assertions, frames built through public rf/make-frame. title: [RULED] Machines: an excellent statecharts implementation, re-frame and ClojureScript native; XState is admired and its features supported natively, not a parity target
description:
## The question

Is XState (v6 direction) a conformance target for re-frame2 machines, or only a vocabulary reference?

This was Open question 6 in the 2026-10 adversarial architecture review. The Opus machines review proposed recasting Spec 005 §Lessons from XState as "vocabulary borrowed from XState". On that basis it proposed deleting the constructs that no example app uses (`:type :choice`, `:timeout`/`:on-timeout`, `:internal-events`, the `:ns/*` tier, history states), about 1,300+ source lines. Sol 11 agreed that "parity does not earn each feature", but it took that position after reading Opus, so it is not independent. Today, `spec/005-StateMachines.md` §Lessons from xstate states the standing rule as "the XState v6 direction is the parity reference; align unless substrate-constrained".

## Ruling (Mike, 2026-10-15 21:1x AUSEST), verbatim

> we think Xstate is state of the art. We aspire to support its fetures but we want to do it in a way that is re-frame native and natural, taking advantage of re-frame's features and ethos.

> Yes, we admire xstate but ultimiately we just want to implement an excellent statecharts implementation that is re-frame and ClojureScript native

## What follows from it

1. **The goal is an excellent statecharts implementation, re-frame and ClojureScript native.** XState is admired as the state of the art and is the reference whose features we aspire to support. It is not a parity target. Neither "align unless substrate-constrained" nor "vocabulary only" is the rule.
2. **Statechart features are supported, not trimmed for lack of callers.** History states, the `:ns/*` partial-descriptor tier, `:choice`, `:timeout`/`:on-timeout` and `:internal-events` all express XState / statechart features, and they stay. The Opus proposal to delete them (machines action 1, "trim the grammar to the re-frame core") is rejected. An absent example caller is not a reason to remove a statechart feature.
3. **Each feature is expressed the re-frame way:**
   - topology as data;
   - keywords and registered ids, never JS-shaped helpers;
   - pure callbacks returning `{:data :fx}`;
   - the per-frame router;
   - managed effects and subscriptions where they fit.

   A divergence from XState needs a reason grounded in that (excellence, nativeness or the re-frame ethos), not only in substrate constraint. A form that mainly copies JavaScript runtime ergonomics stays rejected, as it was already (EP-0029 Group C).
4. **Implementation cost is a separate, open quality question.** For example, `:choice` and `:timeout` are desugared by a scan on every `machine-transition`. Doing that once at registration would be the native fix. That is engineering work, not a grammar question.
5. **Not settled by this ruling (still open):**
   - nil-before-birth: whether views see `nil` or the initial snapshot before the first event. A UX call.
   - sub-vector `:after` delays: a re-frame-native extension (delays read through a subscription) that is not an XState feature, and that crosses machine encapsulation. Sol asked for a separate decision.

The follow-up spec edit is filed as a separate bead (discovered from this one).
close_reason:
RULED (Mike, 2026-10-15): machines aim at an excellent statecharts implementation that is re-frame and ClojureScript native. XState is admired as the state of the art, and its features are ones we aspire to support, but expressed the re-frame way, taking advantage of re-frame's features and ethos. XState is a reference, not a parity target.

Verbatim:
- "we think Xstate is state of the art. We aspire to support its fetures but we want to do it in a way that is re-frame native and natural, taking advantage of re-frame's features and ethos."
- "Yes, we admire xstate but ultimiately we just want to implement an excellent statecharts implementation that is re-frame and ClojureScript native"

Consequences:
- Statechart features stay: history states, `:ns/*`, `:choice`, `:timeout`/`:on-timeout`, `:internal-events`. The proposal to delete them because no example app uses them (Opus machines action 1) is rejected.
- A divergence from XState needs a reason grounded in excellence or re-frame/CLJS nativeness, not only in substrate constraint. JavaScript-runtime-shaped forms stay rejected (EP-0029 Group C).
- Implementation cost, such as the per-transition desugar scans, is an engineering question, not a grammar one.
- Still open: nil-before-birth (a UX call), and the sub-vector `:after` delays (not an XState feature; they cross machine encapsulation).
- Spec 005 §Lessons from xstate still states the superseded rule ("the XState v6 direction is the parity reference; align unless substrate-constrained"). Its correction is the follow-up bead.

title: spec/Runtime-Subsystems describes a capability map and :rf.error/missing-capability that the reference does not have
description:
`spec/Runtime-Subsystems.md` describes, as present behaviour, a capability map and a `:rf.error/missing-capability` error that the reference does not have. A port implementer, or an AI reading the spec, would build to something that does not exist.

## What the spec claims

- §Capability maps (~L271-292) describes a `{:capabilities {:rf.capability/http …}}` map, and says "a required capability that is absent surfaces `:rf.error/missing-capability`" (~L284).
- §Late-bind compatibility calls `late-bind/publish!` / `late-bind/lookup` "a bridge into capabilities".

## What exists

- The late-bind functions are `set-fn!` / `get-fn`; the names in the spec do not exist.
- Nothing implements a capability map. `live_frame.cljc` (~L650) says a supplied `:capabilities` simply flows through as ordinary config.
- `:rf.error/missing-capability` has no emitter and no Spec 009 row.

Other specs already contradict it:
- `spec/008-Testing.md` (~L318): "Instead of injecting a capability map, a hermetic test composes a later image…".
- `spec/Spec-Schemas.md` (~L4329): "no … capability map".

Meanwhile the operational-environment text in Runtime-Subsystems (~L6, 220, 228, 232, 234, 243, 251) and `spec/Ownership.md` (~L72) still list a capability map as a process singleton.

## Change

Rewrite in the present tense: services arrive through late-bind hooks (use the correct names), images, frame config and the adapter. A port MAY add a capability layer under the reserved `:rf.capability/*` namespace.

Leave the Conventions row alone; it is already accurate. This is doc-only.

`spec/Runtime-Subsystems.md` and `spec/Ownership.md` are not hot-zone files.

title: reg-resource and reg-mutation silently accept unknown bare metadata keys; route them through the shared registration-key classifier
description:
`reg-resource` and `reg-mutation` silently accept unknown bare metadata keys, unlike every core `reg-*`. A typo such as `:stale-after` registers and does nothing.

## What core does

Core registrars run their metadata through `re-frame.reg-meta/validate-registration-metadata!` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/reg_meta.cljc` ~L106). That is the Conventions §No silent swallow classifier:
- known and namespaced keys pass;
- an unknown bare key emits the dev warning `:rf.warning/unknown-registration-key`;
- a retired key throws.

## What resources does

`validate-resource-spec!` (`implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/registry.cljc` ~L225) and `validate-mutation-spec!` (`mutation_registry.cljc` ~L59) check required keys and value shapes, but never the key set. The resources artefact never calls the classifier. So a typo, or a deferred key like `:placeholder`, registers and does nothing. Spec 016 (~L818) meanwhile claims the deferred keys are "rejected / unused in v1".

This warning reports a mistake, not legal code, so it is consistent with "warn on failures".

## Change

Route both registrars' metadata through the shared classifier, with resource and mutation vocabularies owned by the resources artefact. An arity taking the vocabulary set is fine; core must not learn resource keys.

The vocabulary must cover every key the code reads, including `:timeout-ms`:
- `ensure-load` reads it to stamp the ledger's `:deadline-at` (`events.cljc` ~L662, `(when-let [ms (:timeout-ms spec)] …)`);
- `docs/api/re-frame.resources.md` (~L803) already lists it.

In Spec 016:
- add `:timeout-ms` to the optional-keys line (~L795), noting that the transport timeout is the `:request` args' own `:timeout-ms`;
- correct ~L818 to say "warns".

Add no hard error, and no check on namespaced keys.

title: Unit-test pruning: resources
description:
Apply the exact requested pruning prompt recursively to implementation/resources/test. This is a distinct worker cluster under rf2-0wcq5. Production code remains unchanged except temporary hash-verified fault plants. Push a draft test-only PR, babysit all latest-head checks to green, then mark ready. A measured no-op or unexecuted-file report is valid; do not manufacture changes.

Simplify the unit tests under implementation/resources/test. Do not change the code under test. LLMs tend to
write too many low-value unit tests, and this suite was largely written by them.

Assume the suite has more tests than it needs, and that many of its tests are longer
than they need to be. Every test costs CI time, reading time and refactoring friction,
and the low-value ones hide the tests that matter. I want a lean suite: each test earns
its place by guarding a behaviour a caller relies on, against a regression that could
plausibly happen and would matter. Each surviving test should be as short as the thing
it proves.

Stay inside implementation/resources/test. Do not edit tests elsewhere. If a deletion relies on a test outside
implementation/resources/test to keep covering something, name that test in your report.

Work in this order:
1. Run the suite and record the result: tests, assertions, failures, lines. Confirm a
   runner actually executes each file in implementation/resources/test; a file nothing runs cannot be pruned on
   evidence, so report it.
2. Read the code under test and list what it promises its callers: normal results, each
   boundary that takes its own path, each promised failure, and any past bug the tests
   refer to.
3. Map every test to the promise it checks. Most of the work shows up in this map:
   promises with five tests, tests with no promise, and tests of something no caller
   relies on.
4. Decide each test: keep, simplify, merge or delete.
5. Run the suite again and prove the pruned suite still guards every promise.

Work in small batches by contract group, and commit as you go. Before each batch,
predict the change in test and assertion counts; after it, confirm the counts moved by
exactly that much. If helper agents are available, use read-only ones for the mapping
step. If implementation/resources/test plainly will not finish in about four hours, stop at a group boundary,
ship what is done, and list the files you did not reach.

Decide each test with two questions:
- If this test were deleted, what bug could ship that no remaining test would catch?
  If you cannot name one, delete it.
- If you can name one: is that bug plausible in this code, would a caller notice it,
  and would nothing else surface it at once (a compile or load error, a boot-time
  validation, most of the suite going red)? If the bug is implausible, harmless, or
  loud anyway, delete the test.

Delete:
- A test another test implies. If A cannot pass while B fails, drop B.
- Extra examples of one behaviour that take the same path through the code.
- Existence and smoke checks: a function exists, a var resolves, something "is
  registered", a result is non-nil, a call "does not throw", when another test
  exercises the same call with a real assertion.
- Change detectors: a test that copies a constant, a data table, a default config, a
  roster or a string out of the source and asserts equality. It fails on every intended
  change and catches no bug. The exception is a value callers depend on exactly, such as
  a public id or a documented default, that nothing else pins: keep one test for it.
- Absence checks for things nothing produces, and negative-input tests for inputs no
  caller passes and the contract does not mention.
- Exhaustive enumeration: one row per enum member, keyword or field when they all take
  one path. Keep one representative plus the members that take a different path.
- Tests of the language, a library or the framework: a constructor sets a field, a
  getter returns it, a map holds the key just put in it.
- Tests that pin how the code works instead of what it does: private helpers already
  exercised through the public path, call order, internal data shapes, greps of the
  implementation's own source, and log, trace or error wording that is not part of the
  contract.
- Tests whose expected value is computed by the same logic as the code under test.
- Assertions that a mock returned what it was told to return, and tests whose mock setup
  is most of the test while the assertion checks the mock.
- Separate per-platform test files asserting the same thing about platform-neutral code.
  A single shared test that runs on both platforms is one test, not two: keep it.
- Tests of test helpers and fixtures.
- Tests of code that has no logic in it, and tests whose only subject is production code
  that no production caller uses.

Simplify every test you keep:
- Assert the whole result with one equality instead of one assertion per field. Drop an
  assertion that a later one in the same test implies.
- Cut setup, fixtures and data to what the assertion needs. Remove unused bindings,
  requires, helpers and fixtures.
- Tests that vary one input become one table-driven test. Keep the boundary rows and
  drop the mid-range ones.
- Tests that repeat the same setup for one assertion each become one test.
- Delete comments and docstrings that restate the code or narrate history. Keep a
  one-line why where a test's purpose is not obvious from its name and body.
- Rename a test only when its name no longer says what it asserts, and first check that
  nothing matches on the name, such as a CI filter, a skip list or a doc that cites it.

Keep, however small:
- The only test of a promise a caller relies on: a normal result, a boundary that takes
  a different path (empty, one, many; zero; the limit and one past it), a promised
  failure.
- A regression test for a bug that actually happened, unless a stronger test now covers
  it.
- The last guard of a security, privacy or redaction promise.
- The last test that keeps a gate able to fail, and the last test holding a published
  doc or spec claim to the code.
When a weak test and a strong test overlap, keep the strong one: the one that would fail
on more bugs.

Do not:
- Weaken an assertion, or swap an exact check for a looser one, to make a merge or a
  simplification easier.
- Delete a test because it fails, is slow or is flaky. Report it.
- Leave unused helpers, fixtures or requires behind.
- Add new tests. If you find a promise with no test, report it.
- Change production code. Dead code and stale docs or spec text go in your report as a
  list, not into your change.
If anything pins test counts or names, such as a count floor or a roster, update it in
the same change. Commit one file or module at a time.

Prove it:
- The suite passes before and after. Report both sets of counts.
- For each group of deletions that rests on a surviving cover, break the code in a place
  the deleted tests guarded and confirm a surviving test fails. Then restore the code and
  confirm it matches the committed file. One plant per group sharing a cover is enough.
  If nothing fails, you removed real coverage: put the tests back.
- A cover must actually run. A skipped test, a fixture the runner never loads, or a test
  on a lane nothing executes covers nothing. Confirm the runner executes a cover before
  resting a deletion on it.
- Run each test file you touched on its own at least once. Deleting a file can break a
  sibling that relied on it loading something first; give such a file its own require.
- A deletion made under the second question needs no plant. Give its one-line reason in
  the report instead.
- A simplification must not change what a test can catch. Where you removed an
  assertion, name the assertion that implies it.

Report:
- Before and after: tests, assertions, lines.
- Deleted tests, grouped by reason. For each, the surviving cover, or the one-line
  reason it was not worth keeping.
- Merges and simplifications: what went into what, and the lines each file lost.
- Notable keeps: tests you considered deleting but kept, and why.
- Plants, and which test caught each.
- Tests outside implementation/resources/test that your deletions rely on.
- Dead code, stale docs or spec text, and gaps (promises with no test). One line each.

If you are unsure whether a promise a caller relies on is still covered, keep the test
and say so. Losing the only guard of a real promise is still the one mistake that matters
more than leaving an extra test in. But being unsure whether a test is worth keeping is
not a reason to keep it. If you cannot say in one line what plausible regression it
catches that a caller would notice, delete it.

title: A queued GC check armed unowned can collect a newly released resource immediately
description:
Merged-PR audit #11299, merge 85676603120f9c187daacf014c0d8a85edcd9ba7. The armed-while-owned? stamp fixes the reported owned-settle FIFO, but a check armed during an ownerless prefetch carries no stamp and can still collect an entry after a later final release re-arms its full GC window.

Reproduced with the PR's virtual host clock, real timer thunk and real router, without shadow-cljs. An ownerless prefetch settles at t=0 with gc-after-ms 1000. At t=900 queue ensure with owner [:app :prefetch-bounce 1], then release-owner for that owner. Fire the original timer at t=1000 before draining. FIFO is [ensure, release-owner, gc-fired]. Instrumenting the real schedule! confirms the ensure arms GC with that owner, and the release arms it owner-free, both at t=1000. The older unstamped gc-fired then deletes the entry at t=1000 and cancels the fresh window; the entry should remain until t=2000. Observed entry-kept-after-new-owner-release=false and entry-kept-through-new-window=false. This is the same public full post-release window guarantee as the source finding.

Make a queued GC check respect the window that authorized it even when that window began unowned and an ensure/release pair intervenes. Keep this internal and preserve deterministic replay. Add the above queued prefetch-to-owner-to-final-release case: entry remains through t=1999 and collects at t=2000. Preserve the existing owned-settle FIFO regression, ordinary ownerless prefetch collection, partial timer re-arming, and server/:never behavior.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY (PR #11317) — already fixed by the GC window (#11310); regression pinned
Reproduced the audit's interleaving as test a-check-queued-behind-an-owners-ensure-and-release-waits-for-its-window in implementation/resources/test/re_frame/resources_gc_queued_check_cljs_test.cljc, using held router drains: an ownerless prefetch settles at t=0 with gc-after-ms 1000; at t=900 an ensure under a new owner is queued, then that owner's release-owner; the settle timer fires at t=1000 before the drain. The test asserts the FIFO [ensure, release-owner, gc-fired], that the entry survives the drain, that it is still cached at t=1999, and that it is collected at t=2000.
GREEN on tip 5c5f9bce5d: the namespace ran 5 tests / 18 assertions, exit 0. The fresh-skip ensure opens a window and so does the final release, so the settle window's check is :superseded.
NOT VACUOUS: planting `superseded? false` in gc-fired-handler turned the namespace red, exit 1, 8 failures. The new test failed at both of its kept-entry assertions, and the three existing queued-check tests failed too. The source was restored and the default-form blob hash matched the committed blob.

title: CI classifier: scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh arms no job, so widening epoch's prod-gate exclusions runs unwatched
description:
The change classifier's production-gate arm lists only three of the four prod-gate roster scripts. A PR that edits only `scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh`, including one that WIDENS epoch's exclusion roster, therefore schedules no `jvm-epoch-prod-gate` job. This is the silent coverage loss the arm exists to prevent.

## Evidence (trunk 89517e8f54)

`.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh:771`:

    scripts/test-core-prod-gate.sh|scripts/test-routing-prod-gate.sh|scripts/test-ssr-prod-gate.sh)

Its comment (L772-779) gives the reason: each script IS a production-gate lane's roster, and "the one edit that can silently REMOVE coverage (widening the exclusions) would otherwise fire no job at all". It then says "One flag covers all three".

There are four such scripts: `scripts/test-{core,routing,ssr,epoch}-prod-gate.sh`. `.github/workflows/test.yml:2663` defines `jvm-epoch-prod-gate`, gated at L2667 on `needs.detect_changed_surfaces.outputs.implementation_jvm == 'true'`, and running `bash scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh` (L2700). The test.yml comment at L2652-2662 says epoch's roster is the lopsided one: an exclusion list of about 22 namespaces that is not expected to empty. It is the roster most likely to be widened.

**Measured.** A dossier worker ran the classifier on the epoch path alone, `report-changed-surfaces.sh scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh`. It exited 0 with every output false. The routing script, run as a control, armed `implementation_jvm`. Nothing in `implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs` pins this arm.

## Change

- Add `scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh` to the L771 alternation, and make the comment's count say four.
- In the same commit, pin the arm in `implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs`: each of the four roster scripts, alone, arms `implementation_jvm`.

**HOT ZONE.** The classifier and its test mirror pin each other, so both move in ONE commit. Sequence this after any other bead touching that pair.

Supporting detail, local to this machine only: `C:\Users\miket\code\re-frame2\ai\decisions\tooling-invariants-and-lane-registry.md`.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Running `report-changed-surfaces.sh scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh` prints `implementation_jvm=true`.
2. `_changed-surfaces.test.cjs` pins all four prod-gate roster scripts. Removing any one from the arm turns the test red; check this with a planted fault.
3. The classifier and its mirror change in one commit, and `npm run test:scripts` stays green.
notes:

- `report-changed-surfaces.sh` prod-gate arm now lists all four roster scripts (`scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh` added; comment says "all four").
- `_changed-surfaces.test.cjs` pins it: a pinnedRoster of `scripts/test-{core,routing,ssr,epoch}-prod-gate.sh` plus a test that each, classified alone, arms implementation_jvm. One commit, both files.
- Measured: `report-changed-surfaces.sh scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh` printed implementation_jvm=false on trunk (routing control true) and implementation_jvm=true on the branch, exit 0 both.
- Plant (epoch removed from the alternation): the test file exited 1, failing only the new test on the epoch line; restored by blob hash match, rerun exit 0, 105 passed.
- `npm run test:scripts` locally on Windows: exit 1, 5 environment-bound failures (preflight package tests, rewrite-local-root-coord, check_modules_compile) in files that reference neither the classifier nor any prod-gate script; CI's unconditional js-harness-self-tests job is the evidence for acceptance criterion 3.

In one commit: .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh's prod-gate arm now lists scripts/test-epoch-prod-gate.sh with the other three roster scripts, and its comment says four; implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs pins the arm, so each of the four roster scripts, classified alone, arms implementation_jvm. title: Emit the :large size marker over a subtree holding a :sensitive leaf, measured after redaction, instead of shipping the subtree raw
description:
## Ruling

When a `:large` declaration covers a subtree that holds a `:sensitive` descendant, the walker emits the ordinary `:rf.size/large-elided` marker at the large node. Its `:bytes`, and its `:digest` when digests are enabled, are computed over the subtree AFTER its sensitive descendants have been redacted. Each declaration then keeps its own meaning. `:large` always means "marker plus handle". `:sensitive` always means "never revealed, not even by a measurement". With the public data and structure held fixed, changing a secret's content or length leaves the whole marker unchanged. Sensitive at the same path, or at an ancestor, still wins outright with `:rf/redacted` and no marker. A caller that opted out of sensitive redaction (`:rf.egress/include-sensitive? true`) still gets a marker over the raw subtree, exactly as today.

Worked example. An author declares `:large [[:session]]` and `:sensitive [[:session :refresh-token]]`. Today the `:rf.event/db-pending` trace ships the whole session (a 2,000-item `:inbox-cache` included) with only the token redacted. After this change it ships `{:session {:rf.size/large-elided {:path [:session] :bytes <size of the session with the token already :rf/redacted> :type :map :reason :effect :hint nil :handle [:rf.elision/at [:session]]}}}`. That is exactly what `:large [[:session]]` alone produces.

Decided 2026-10-16: Mike directed that every dossier recommendation an independent Codex review agreed with be actioned. His instruction, verbatim:

> review all decisions. They now have a "Codex Recomendation" section.  Where the original recomendation matches the Code Recomendation, create a bead to action the decision.  And then remove the file.  Leave behind cases where the two differ materially.

The dossier and the Codex review both chose this option (C), with the same scope. Both keep sensitive-wins at the same path. Neither adds a collision warning, a new marker kind or a traversal redesign.

Decisive facts, read in source at trunk 89517e8f54 (the cited files are unchanged at 3aaacf1cde):

1. **Both walkers switch `:large` off for the whole subtree today.** The durable/runtime-db walker's "nested-axis suppression" arm returns `walk-recur` (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/elision.cljc:1043-1046`). The transient walker's arm does the same (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/classification.cljc:331-337`). So every public sibling of the secret ships raw on every trace. Three places pin this: `implementation/core/test/re_frame/elision_test.clj:128-132` (`{:a {:b :rf/redacted :c "public"}}`), `implementation/core/test/re_frame/projection_cljs_test.cljc:172-181`, and `spec/conformance/fixtures/data-classification-nested-large-over-sensitive-redacts.edn:55-68`.
2. **The AI pair overflows, and Spec 009 is contradicted.** A large public sibling makes `get-path [:session]` exceed the 5,000-token default cap (`tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/overflow.cljc:25-28`). The cap then replaces the WHOLE response with `{:rf.mcp/overflow …}` (`tools/mcp-base/src/re_frame/mcp_base/cap.cljc:4-9`), so the agent learns nothing. Spec 009 says that a read at or below a `:large` declaration elides (`spec/009-Instrumentation.md:2908`, `:2911`), and so does the pair's own docstring (`tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/elision.cljs:12-15`). Below a collision node, it does not.
3. **The normative sentence is ambiguous.** `spec/015-Data-Classification.md:451` and `docs/EP/EP-0025-data-classification.md:222-224` say that the subtree "redacts rather than showing a size preview". Read literally, that is whole-subtree redaction, while the code does descend-and-ship. It needs rewording whatever the ruling.

Rejected options:
- **A. Leave it** (descend, redact the leaf, ship the rest raw). This silently switches the large declaration off for the whole subtree, including a finer `:large` added beside the coarse one. Trace and pair payloads stay unbounded, and 009:2908 stays false.
- **B. Redact the whole subtree to `:rf/redacted`.** It is the cheapest change, one line per walker. But it presents public data as a non-expandable secret with no size and no handle. An `elision false` read would then "expand" a `:rf/redacted`, against the display contract at `spec/015-Data-Classification.md:429`.
- **A dev warning on the collision.** It is a nagging diagnostic, and "trust the programmer" rules it out.
- **A new marker kind, or an optional `:bytes`.** It is new surface that this ruling makes unnecessary.
- **A selective-traversal redesign.** That is separate work, not part of this.

Supersedes: the nested-axis suppression rule in EP-0025 §Egress rules (`docs/EP/EP-0025-data-classification.md:222-224`) and in Spec 015 §No propagation (`spec/015-Data-Classification.md:451`). It also revises the closed rf2-3x7nj.4.1, which made the offset replay "descend at a shadowing ancestor". No standing ruling bead covers this collision.

## Work

**Code** (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/`):
- `elision.cljc:1043-1046` (the durable/runtime-db walker). The nested-axis arm returns a marker for the node instead of `walk-recur`. Walk the subtree with large elision disabled and sensitive redaction in force, so its sensitive descendants redact. Then build the marker (`->marker`, `elision.cljc:680-697`) over that redacted result, with the node's own path, reason and hint. When digests are enabled, compute the `:digest` over the same redacted value. Keep existing-marker idempotence: a value that is already a marker passes through the new arm unchanged, as it does in the ordinary marker arm that follows.
- `elision.cljc:1146-1156` (the offset replay for `get-path` and `project-egress :path`). Today, when a shadowing ancestor's decide returns `walk-recur`, the loop descends. Under this ruling the ancestor must not build its marker from the ancestor's candidates over the slice. Replay the candidate set all the way to the read's own coordinate, keep sensitive-ancestor precedence (a sensitive ancestor still returns `:rf/redacted`), and then wrap the slice as a marker at the read path, measured after redacting the slice's own sensitive descendants. A read with `:rf.egress/include-large? true` returns the slice with only its sensitive descendants redacted.
- `classification.cljc:331-337` (the transient walker, which covers event args, fx args, cofx and sub output). Make the same change: return `(large-marker <v walked with large disabled> path)` instead of `walk-recur`.
- Rewrite in present tense the docstrings and comments that describe the suppression: `elision.cljc:978-994` (`large-keys-shadowing-sensitive`), `:1028-1042`, `:1109-1113` and `:1141-1145`, and `classification.cljc:233-244` (`large-shadow-set`) and `:296-301`. They cite "Spec 015 §No-propagation (L338), a normative MUST", which no longer exists. Cite 015 §No propagation and 009 §Wire marker instead. The shadow sets are still needed, because they mark where a marker has to be measured after redaction, so keep them, renamed if that reads better.

**Tests** (flip three, add two):
- `implementation/core/test/re_frame/elision_test.clj:128-132`. Expect a marker at `[:a]` whose `:bytes` equals the pr-str byte count of `{:b :rf/redacted :c "public"}`. With `:rf.egress/include-large? true`, expect `{:a {:b :rf/redacted :c "public"}}`.
- `elision_test.clj:299-303` (`offset-read-below-a-shadowing-large-ancestor-…`). A read at `[:a :x]` returns a marker with `:path [:a :x]`. With the size override it returns `{:secret :rf/redacted :pub "ok"}`. A direct read of `[:a :x :secret]` still returns `:rf/redacted`, with or without the size override.

title: CEDN-1 unpaired-surrogate rejection: golden error row, and three callers that still assume text always encodes
description:
rf2-626f1 made the CEDN-1 encoder reject text holding an unpaired surrogate. canonical-bytes and canonical now throw :rf.error/non-edn-identity, reason :unpaired-surrogate, for a string, or a keyword or symbol namespace or name, holding one. Four places outside that change's fence still assume the old behaviour. Each is small and none changes behaviour that matters today:

1. Golden error row. The corpus cannot pin the rejection yet. In spec/conformance/fixture-file.edn the :canonical-bytes call is a closed map whose :expect (a :string) is required and which has no :expect-error, and the reference runner's :canonical-bytes entry (implementation/core/test/re_frame/conformance_runner.cljc) carries only the :expect matcher. Change: make :expect optional, add an optional :expect-error :keyword under the :thrown-error-id law (the shape :path-instantiate already uses), add `:expect-error thrown-error-id` to the runner's :canonical-bytes matchers, then add a row such as {:call :canonical-bytes :value "a\uD800b" :expect-error :rf.error/non-edn-identity} to cedn1-path-algebra-golden.edn. The EDN reader turns the \uD800 escape into the lone unit, so the fixture file itself stays valid UTF-8. Mention the op's error form in spec/conformance/README.md if that file lists op shapes.

2. implementation/core/src/re_frame/path.cljc segment? admits every string, keyword and symbol, so the shared segment upper bound is now wider than the CEDN-1 domain for text holding an unpaired surrogate, against its own docstring ("the shared path vocabulary MUST NOT be wider than canonical EDN identity"). Such a segment passes normalize-concrete and fails closed later, wherever canonical-bytes runs over the path (schema digest). Decide whether segment? also checks text, at the cost of a scan per string segment, or whether the docstring and Conventions §Path shape and segment domain state the narrower claim.

3. implementation/routing/src/re_frame/routing/registry.cljc url-value-refusal: the comment on its admitted-scalar fast path says rf.identity/encode cannot reject a string, keyword or symbol. It now can. Behaviour is still a refusal, because route-url's URL encoder already refuses an unpaired surrogate (routing/url.cljc on the JVM, encodeURIComponent on CLJS), so only the comment is stale.

4. implementation/resources/src/re_frame/resources/ssr.cljc utf8-bytes maps an unpaired surrogate to ? for JVM/CLJS fnv parity. Its only input is canonical-bytes output, which can no longer hold one, so that branch is unreachable, and the fnv-1a-32 docstring's mention of an unpaired-surrogate fixture case does not match the test. Delete the branch or keep it as defence, and make the docstring true.
notes:

title: Honor :on-recoverable-error on Fresco hydrating roots
description:
PR #11442 (6242e161f9a010d040f0f920cc65d5d4d4ed62ec) makes React adoption the sole hydration-mismatch channel. Its revised spec/011-SSR.md:674 promises every React-family root composes the framework reporter over the host's :on-recoverable-error; :1212 directs CI to mount with {:hydrate? true :on-recoverable-error (fn [error info] ...)}. Fresco is explicitly included in the preceding root roster.

That recipe cannot boot a Fresco root. implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/mount.cljs:128-138 admits only :hydrate? and :identifier-prefix, and render-client-root! calls require-root-options! at :585 before mounting. Adding the documented callback raises :rf.error/fresco-unknown-root-option, naming :on-recoverable-error. Further, hydrate-root-options at :356-364 always installs (hydration-reporter window frame-kw), whose callback at :347-354 delegates only to report-recoverable-default!; merely admitting the key would still leave the host callback unused.

Focused evidence: evaluated the actual merged root-options-roster, frame-config-keys and require-root-options! forms with only fail! replaced by an ex-info stub. {:hydrate? true :identifier-prefix "main"} was accepted; {:hydrate? true :on-recoverable-error (fn [_ _])} raised {:rf.error/id :rf.error/fresco-unknown-root-option :option :on-recoverable-error}. Probe exit 0; ai/pr-audit/pr-audit-sol-oct11-11442-callback-1.log and matching .exit record it. No shadow-cljs lane was entered. The Reagent/UIx spine already composes the same public callback correctly; rf2-mn2ht.44's completed Reagent/slim work was read as precedent, not reused as a finding.

Small correction: admit :on-recoverable-error on Fresco's root options, pass it through the hydrating door, and compose the framework's window-bounded record/trace first, then the authored callback (preserving React's default when absent). Update the root-options documentation. A mounted hydration regression should show the callback called once for a real recoverable mismatch while the existing trace and always-on record remain; a post-window recovery should still delegate without a hydration label.
notes:
== WORKER SUMMARY (PR #11455, branch worker/ssr-fresco-hydration, commit 9b1b0edf16) ==
Done. Fresco's root door admits :on-recoverable-error (roster #{:hydrate? :identifier-prefix :on-recoverable-error}). impl.mount/hydration-reporter takes the host callback as a third argument and composes as the spine's native-hydration-reporter does: inside the adoption window it fans the always-on record and emits the dev trace, then calls the host callback (or React's default report when none); after the window it calls the callback alone. title: Worker pre-commit beads boundary refuses a conflict-resolved merge of origin/main
description:
In a worker worktree, the pre-commit worker beads boundary (scripts/git-hooks/lib/check-beads-boundary.sh, called from scripts/git-hooks/pre-commit) refuses the commit that finishes a CONFLICTED merge of origin/main. The hook reads `git diff --cached --name-only`, which compares the index with HEAD, the branch's first parent. Main's own `.beads/issues.jsonl` therefore shows up as a "staged beads-database path", even though the merge only takes main's version and the PR diff (merge-base..HEAD, what scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh grades) carries no .beads change.

A conflict-free `git merge origin/main` is never checked, because git runs pre-merge-commit (not installed) rather than pre-commit, so this only bites when a merge needs resolving. The hook's printed remedy (`git restore --staged .beads; git checkout HEAD -- .beads`) would be wrong in that case: the merge would keep the branch's stale export, and the PR diff would then revert main's tracker changes.

Measured on worker/static-flows, 2026-10-17: the merge of f8aadd8639 conflicted in two prose rows, and the finishing `git commit` was refused, naming .beads/issues.jsonl. The worker worked around it without skipping the hook. It first committed main's text for the two conflicting rows, then took the one remaining conflict hunk with `-X ours`, so git created the merge commit itself.

A possible fix: when MERGE_HEAD exists, refuse only .beads paths whose staged blob differs from BOTH parents (or from MERGE_HEAD's), since taking main's export is exactly what a worker merge should do. Add a case to scripts/git-hooks/test-pre-commit.sh.
notes:
== FIX (PR #11470, branch worker/beads-hook-merge)

The fix is in scripts/git-hooks/lib/check-beads-boundary.sh, in commit context only. While MERGE_HEAD exists, a .beads database path whose staged blob equals MERGE_HEAD's blob (or which is absent from both) passes. One equal to neither parent is still refused. The merge-case refusal heads its list "Staged beads-database paths matching neither side of this merge:" and prints, per path, `git restore --source=MERGE_HEAD --staged --worktree -- <path>` as the remedy, never `git checkout HEAD -- .beads`. Every other case is unchanged: ordinary commits (same message), the mayor checkout (the block no-ops there), the config allow-list, and the CI arm (ci context never consults MERGE_HEAD).

No reinstall is needed. The managed pre-commit block is byte-identical, so `install-git-hooks.sh --check` exits 0 and no pin moves. The installed block sources the lib from the committing worktree.

Tests: test-pre-commit.sh layer 4 gains (m1), (m2), (m2-remedy) and (m3).
- (m1): conflicted merge, tracker as the merge took it from main. Passes, and the PR diff carries no tracker change.
- (m2): staged tracker equal to neither parent. Refused with the MERGE_HEAD remedy. Running that remedy concludes the merge.
- (m3): an ordinary commit staging main's very export. Still refused with the ordinary remedy, so a fix that compared against main rather than MERGE_HEAD fails it.

Measured runs:
- On the unfixed lib: 92 passed, 3 failed, exit 1. (m1) and both (m2) cases failed; (m3) passed.
- With the fix: 95 passed, 0 failed, exit 0.

scripts/git-hooks/README.md gains a "Concluding a merge of main" subsection and test rows 39-41. CLAUDE.md does not quote the hook's remedy, so it is unchanged.
close_reason: Merged in #11470 (three commits on ed5d90d496, head 3f187e2db9). scripts/git-hooks/lib/check-beads-boundary.sh, in commit context only: while MERGE_HEAD exists, a staged beads-database path passes if its blob equals MERGE_HEAD's blob for that path (or the path is absent from both), and a blob equal to neither parent is still refused. The merge-case message lists the offending paths and prints `git restore --source=MERGE_HEAD --staged --worktree -- <path>` per path, never `git checkout HEAD -- .beads`, and explains why the --theirs/--ours rule does not apply to a worker merge. Ordinary commits (same message), the mayor checkout, the config allow-list and the CI arm (which never reads MERGE_HEAD) are unchanged; the managed pre-commit block is byte-identical, so install-git-hooks.sh --check exits 0 and every checkout picks up the fix from its own lib with no reinstall. scripts/git-hooks/README.md gains "Concluding a merge of main" and test rows 39-41. Evidence: new layer-4 cases in test-pre-commit.sh, (m1) a conflicted merge taking main's export passes with no tracker change in the PR diff, (m2) a blob equal to neither parent is refused with the MERGE_HEAD remedy and that remedy concludes the merge, (m3) outside a merge, staging main's exact export is still refused; against the unfixed lib 92 passed / 3 failed (m1 and both m2 checks) exit 1, with the fix 95 passed / 0 failed exit 0, including layer 5 (check-beads-pr-boundary.sh's own test); CI 59 checks, 0 failed, PR guards log shows 95 passed. Residuals recorded on the bead: the 90% truncation floor still compares the staged tracker with HEAD, so a worker merge taking a main export more than 10% smaller than the branch's would still be refused (rare); a merge that keeps HEAD's stale export is not staged relative to HEAD and is caught by the CI arm instead.

title: Image assembly: probe the generation cache before flattening the descriptor store
description:
## Current

`assemble`'s live-store arity evaluates `(source-store-descriptors)` before `assemble-cached` probes its cache, and that call flattens every retained descriptor (`implementation/core/src/re_frame/image_assembly.cljc` ~1676-1680, and the 0-arity default at ~1736-1740; the probe is at ~1574-1576).

So every explicit-image `make-frame` walks the whole store, even on a cache hit. A frame made without `:images` assembles nothing and is unaffected.

## Change

Pass the pool as a thunk, or something equivalent, that `assemble-cached` calls only on a miss. Keep identical-object reuse on a hit and the existing invalidation. If this cannot be done without complicating the cache, stop and say so in the close reason.

## Acceptance

A test shows that a cache hit never calls the store flattener, and the existing image-assembly tests stay green.

Checked at trunk f4e5adad0a.
notes:
== DONE (worker core-internals, 2026-10-19, PR #11504, branch worker/core-internals) ==

Premise held at tip 560f3b2829. Both live-store call sites (assemble's explicit-image arity and assemble-default's 0-arity) evaluated (source-store-descriptors) as an argument before assemble-cached probed generation-cache.

Change: assemble-cached takes the pool as a zero-arg pool-fn and calls it only on a miss. The live-store arities pass source-store-descriptors itself, and the explicit-pool arities pass (constantly descriptors). The cache key, identical-object reuse on a hit, superseded-entry eviction and invalidation are untouched, so this did not complicate the cache. A side effect is that the live-store pool is now read after the store generation, which matches the existing comment "Read it BEFORE selecting".

Test: a-cache-hit-never-flattens-the-store in image_assembly_cache_cljs_test.cljc, which runs on the JVM and in CLJS. It wraps rf.source-store/kinds-present in a counter and requires an explicit-image hit and a default-image hit to make 0 calls. As the instrument's control, it then requires the miss after a new registration to make exactly 1 call.

Evidence: the namespace ran 13 tests and 14 assertions, 0 failures, on the JVM (12 and 13 before; +1 and +1 as predicted). Sabotage: the explicit-image live call site was planted with (constantly (source-store-descriptors)), restoring the eager read. The namespace then exited 1, with this test alone failing (actual [[true true 1] 1]). The restore was verified by blob hash against HEAD (default form match) and by git diff --quiet. The fast-PR spine exited 0 (JVM core 1186 / 3591; test:cljs 6150 / 17322). The CLJS run proves the instrument fired there too, because the control half needs the redef to count the miss.
close_reason: Merged in #11504. assemble-cached (implementation/core/src/re_frame/image_assembly.cljc) now takes a zero-arg pool-fn and calls it only on a miss. The live-store paths pass source-store-descriptors, and the explicit-pool paths pass (constantly descriptors). The cache key, the reuse of the identical object on a hit, eviction and invalidation are unchanged. New test a-cache-hit-never-flattens-the-store: an explicit-image hit and a default-image hit make 0 flattener calls, and a control miss makes exactly 1. JVM namespace run: 13 tests, 14 assertions, exit 0 (+1/+1 as predicted). With the eager read put back at the call site it exited 1, with only that test failing.

title: Read-attribution reproduction builds but aborts because its rig has no image generation
description:

It cannot produce the advertised read-attribution measurements.

Evidence: read the full rf2-9ifla record and PR body, which report the successful 132-file build followed by that actual forward-run failure. Independent source inspection at the merge shows build-rig! in implementation/core/test/re_frame/bench/read_attribution_cljs.cljs creates the frame as (rf.live-frame/make-frame {:id fid}) at line 1257 and records frame-resolution-generation in :gen at line 1296. The -main precondition at lines 1377-1383 throws whenever :gen is nil. live_frame.cljc lines 451-462 explicitly returns nil for a frame made without :images, so this rig cannot reach its measurement arms under the current frame contract. This is an existing probe defect newly exposed by fixing the compiler recipe; it is not a failure of the new EDN reader.

Small correction: align the rig with the frame/image branch the binding arm intends to measure, preserving its registration inputs and the generation precondition; if that arm is obsolete, retire it and make the reproduction instructions describe the supported measurements instead.
